text: Let me just say that I love having rich friends...from borrowing their sleds to getting to use their Centurion cards when they're not looking...the ancillary benefits of having ballers on your team simply put, rocks. That said, I recently found myself three knuckles deep in a meeting in Santa Barbara when suddenly one of the attendees, a rich friend, announced his stomach was becoming self-loathing and that unless we wanted to see him disintegrate before our very eyes that we chow down ASAFP. Now, for those who don't know, there's an unwritten rule with dudes when it comes to food: whoever invites, provides. Meaning, whoever calls the ball is obligated to quarterback, which in this case means the rich friend is now obligated to pay for lunch. Sunny Santa Barbara, good pals, and free food...my fellow Yelpers, the only thing that could have made this go any better is one Tila Tequila, but she doesn't roll in the 805 so near perfection would have to suffice. So we scurry out of the meeting and since I'm the senior of the group, I call shotgun and send my two underlings to the rear of my rich buddy's Rolls. As I sink in the redonkulously comfortable leather seats of his Phantom, I realize that I'm BASKING in room and comfort and immediately determine that I should do everything I can to extend this ride for as long as possible. It's at this point that my focus has gone from grub to club: I wanted to party because how often do you find yourself in a half-million dollar car with a player who loves to spend money? Exactly...you've got to strike while the iron's hot...especially when the iron is murdered out and worth more than your entire net worth. So I suggest we skip sushi (take it easy...SB blows for sushi and I had a plan) but instead take advantage of the environment and after some subliminal mind freeqing of my buddies, I get them all to agree in harmony, like an experienced barbershop quartet, that Mexican food makes perfect sense and when it comes to Mexican food in SB, there's only one spot to visit: Los Arroyos (LA) in Montecito. Not only did this secure me an additional 40-50 minutes of kicking it in my friend's RR, but it also meant that I could go big for lunch since I didn't have to drive and had ample room to stretch my legs, and belly, after the impending feast. Now unanimously motivated for LA, we arrive and after a few minutes of negotiating his beast in to a parking space, we empty out to the mean streets of Montecito for some authentic south of the border cuisine. Upon our arrival we were greeted by a professional staff (mostly Mexican dudes) that actually had personalities and were a hoot to interact with. Now I'm sure some of you will take that comment as "racist", but being that most of you who are reading this prolly don't think before you...think...go ahead and tell me about the last time you ate at a Mexican joint and actually had a real Mexican talk to you like you were a friend... 'Nuff said. So I ask my wealthy friend what he eats here and his reply was short and sweet: everything. After some prodding, he suggests a dish that's off the menu (the burrito mojado with shredded beef AND steak) that was nearly 3lbs of gooey burrito goodness that made my body wince upon site of "la banquete" that would be placed before me minutes later. But as we were waiting for the main dishes to arrive, we enjoyed freshly made chips with a selection of salsas coupled with guacamole that rivaled the green goo from The Gardens in Westwood. Within minutes I found myself retreating from the conversation and immersing myself in to their chips and dips which were the textbook definition of addictive. After inhaling 2+ baskets of chips, our main dishes arrive and if I had to pick a single word to describe what was descending upon my setting, it would be WOW. Look, I've never been to a Mexican spot where I was dazzled by the presentation of the food, and LA has kept that record in tact, but when I see a clean plate with enough food on it to force the waiter to hold just one plate per hand, it makes the snob in me take a back seat to the wild dingo-inspired chow down that beckoned. And as usual with LA, the steak matches the sizzle as the dish was brimming with flavors that thoroughly challenged my satiety as I was bursting at the seams while still wanting more. I also managed to sneak tastes of my friend's dishes that ranged from fish to chicken to cheese and they all popped...clearly LA knows how to cha cha cha in the kitchen. And then, just a mere 40 minutes later, the smoke settled and the frenzy was over. The four of us left fat and happy and my rich buddy got out of there for under $100, tax and tip included. So if you find yourself in southern SB/Montecito with a hankering for some killer Mexican food, make the time to visit LA because Belinda Carlisle was right: Heaven IS a place on Earth and it's called Los Arroyos. ¡Disfrute de!

text: Patterson House is the swankiest bar I've ever been to. From the subtly marked door, to the classy drinks, to the impeccable service. The Patterson House was originally the house of a governor of Tennessee who vetoed statewide prohibition but was subsequently overruled by the legislature. The location is just a small house with small lettering on the door on a dark street near music row. You walk in and there is a vestibule with a fireplace and a bookshelf. In two frames are the "rules" of the house. This isn't the kind of bar where you can mill about and talk on your phone. You must have a seat to get a drink and you're not allowed to talk on the phone. They say right out front that this isn't the place for your Jaeger bombs and Bud Light. In the middle of the place is the square bar. The bartenders behind the bar are quickly making drinks. These aren't your typical drinks. You see them using fresh mint or raw eggs and there's a plate of citrus on the bar. The bartenders flip bottles, slice, dice, and shake furiously so you get the best drink of your life. They look classy in their ties and vests, much like you just walked into a speakeasy from 1927 but with an updated look. The decor is beautiful with chandeliers and subtle lighting. A server escorts you to your seat. Then you're given a plain clear bottle of water at your table and simple juice glasses. The menus are parchment tied with ribbon. The drinks are divided by liquor: whisky, gin, vodka, rum, brandy, cordials. Then there is a list of some classic cocktails and some food. The cocktails are unlike anything you've seen before. It's a good thing the servers know their stuff, because you may have a lot of questions, and they have all the answers. I could go on and on about this place, but you need to go experience it yourself. If you don't want to pay a high price for an amazing unique drink, then this is not the place for you. The drinks are expensive. The liquors and their combinations are weird. They don't have any of the typical liquors you'd find at a normal bar. If this isn't your scene, that's ok. If you're looking for a hip, unique experience, then you will enjoy the Patterson House.

text: For many years, my family and I, 1st generation Vietnamese immigrants, have been coming to Pho Tau Bay. We loved the food, the warmth, and the way it brought Vietnamese immigrants together over a hot bowl of pho. Over the past few years, however, PTB has lost its genuine Vietnamese charm, prioritizing American approval over Vietnamese solidarity. The past few times I have been to PTB have been extremely disappointing. When I try to speak Vietnamese to people on the staff (the ones that are obviously Vietnamese), they curtly respond in English. One waitress won't even acknowledge me when I place my order in Vietnamese. But to their American clientele, they are courteous and attentive. The servers I've had come to my table twice--once to take my order and once to bring the food. No refills, no courtesy check-ups, nothing. People remark about how cheap PTB is, but if you compare their portion sizes to other Vietnamese restaurants in the New Orleans area, it's not that great of a deal. The pho bowls are small and they give you more broth than anything else. If you look closely, you'll notice that very few Vietnamese people eat here these days. It's because all of them have noticed the same thing I have: we are no longer wanted here. Realizing this, I will no longer eat at PTB, but instead at its Westbank rivals, Tan Dinh or Pho Hoa, or the lesser-known restaurants in New Orleans East, Dong Phuong, Pho Bang, & Ba Mien, where most of the waitstaff still speak to me in my native tongue. Please don't get me wrong, I'm not discrediting the food at PTB. The dishes are delicious. It's why I've been going there since I was 8, why I referred it to so many of my American friends, why I still decided to give it the benefit of the doubt despite feeling unwanted there, why I gave it two stars instead of one. But I'm Vietnamese. When I eat a bowl of bun bo hue or some goi cuon, I want to feel like I'm home. And that place is no longer with Pho Tau Bay.

text: I loved Jones! I went this past Saturday when I was back in town to celebrate my birthday with my family. I chose to come to Jones for dinner, having heard about it before, and knowing my brother comes here often with his friends. The way I see Jones, and similar restaurants (i.e. other Starr restaurants) is that you're coming here not only to get a meal, but to also have an experience. You are going to this particular restaurant because of the unique atsmosphere. That said, I also expect the food to be good with decent sized portions. Upon entering Jones we were seated right away. This was about 5:30/6 on a Saturday night. The place was pretty full, but obviously not packed since we got a booth for 5 with no wait. We sat 2 on one side, 3 on the other in our booth. It was comfortable for my parents on their side, however elbow room was a bit tight for the 3 of us sitting on the other side. It wasn't as tight as some people have described it, though. I wasn't at all uncomfortable; it just made it difficult when we all needed to cut our food at the same time. This was not a huge deal. Theme: The décor of Jones is exactly how others have described it: retro 70's, complete with avocado green booths, wood paneling, orange chairs and funky lighting fixtures. I absolutely loved it. Menu: While the menu is not huge, there are certainly a number of meals to choose from, as well as a wide variety of food from seafood, steak, pasta, and typical favorites like chicken pot pie and meatloaf. There are also a bunch of sandwiches as well. Menu is available on their website. Service: Despite what some may have said about their service, we had no problems. Our waitress even brought my dad's half eaten meal back under the heat lamp to keep warm while he got up to take an important call. Either way, I try not to judge a place based on their service unless I've gone a few times and still have a problem. You can get a bad/snobbish/inattentive server anywhere, from a 5 star restaurant to a local dive, and unfortunately unless you address that with the server or manager, it may not change. But again, we had no issues, just good service. Food: All of us were happy with the food. First of all, the portions were large so I felt the prices were justified. Secondly, despite what I've read on here, I would not put the quality of this food in the same range as a diner - it's most definitely above. While the menu items may have included diner-type meals, you can't forget that it's a part of the theme of this place. What would a retro-themed restaurant be without serving those at-home favorites? The quality of food was what I would expect for the price and type of restaurant. The 5 of us shared two orders of the pierogies as an appetizer. We all raved about how good they were, I definitely recommend them. However, while I found all the portions to be large on other foods, there were only 3 pierogies to an order. Slightly pricey for only 3, but I would order them again because they were that good. For dinner, my mom ordered the chicken pot pie which she was unable to finish due to the size. My dad ordered the pistachio crusted tilapia, and my boyfriend had the spicy jambalaya (and loved it). I went with the make your own salad - there were so many things on the menu that I wanted, but I've been on a major salad kick lately, and when I saw how huge the salads were, I was sold. I have to say, the mini clipboard/checklist sitting on the table for ordering the personal salad was a cute touch as well. Lastly, my brother, who has been here many times, never ordering the same thing twice, tried a hamburger this time. He admits that it was not the most flavorful hamburger and won't order it again, but still loves everything else he's eaten here (including the crabcake which I was considering ordering). Dessert: My dad and I each ordered the strawberry shortcake -delicious, and the boys each ordered the chocolate cake, which was actually served with a cold glass of milk. A cute idea and perfect touch! It's safe to say that I'd like to go to Jones again when I'm back in my home area sometime. I enjoyed the food, the atmosphere was fun and unique, and the prices were pretty much what they should be for this type of place. The dress code can range from casual to dressy, meaning whatever you wear in that range you'd fit in. I recommend Jones if you're looking for a fun place to get a good meal in the city.

text: The Moolah is an awesome theater, and pretty much a must for the latest blockbuster, in-your-face, thrill-a-minute joyrides. But it's not perfect. Here's the rundown: - Seating: Yes, they have leather couches laid out on the floor. They also have traditional theater-style seating in the back, and also a nice balcony area upstairs if you need a little more room. But here's the rub. If you actually want to sit on those couches you need to get there early. Early as in stand-in-line-for-15-minutes-or-more-before-they-allow-people-into-the-theater early. You might get lucky on a weeknight, but this is a definite on the weekends. It isn't like a normal movie theater where you can swoop in at the last minute and still get a halfway decent seat. If you do that here, you will either be relegated to the back or get stuck at a bad angle. Think of it more like going to a concert. Oh, and about those couches. They're nice, but not exactly top of the line stuff...or at least not anymore. Many of them need to be replaced or have been repaired cheaply with tape. They're lumpy and saggy from the thousands of times they've been sat in. Don't get me wrong, they're still better than normal theater seats, but you're not exactly walking into a furniture store here, more like your uncle's old basement. - Concessions: Great stuff. Good beverage selection (alcohol and non-alcohol) as well as relatively inexpensive standard fare like popcorn and candy. Nothing too fancy, but it gets the job done. - Parking: Hoo boy. Alright, well there's a really narrow alleyway behind the theater that leads to a parking garage where you're supposed to park. Sometimes there's a guy at the gate, sometimes there's not. Sometimes he gives you a ticket to put in your car, sometimes he doesn't. Sometimes you're worried that if you return either the gates will be down for good or your car will be gone. Not completely ideal, but I've never had to pay to park and never had a problem. Just a heads-up on what to expect. - Staff - Friendlier than a movie theater staff should be. Don't get me wrong, they're still pimply-faced teenagers, but they're pimply-faced teenagers who smile and actually help you instead of mumbling under their breath or texting their friends. - Overall - Again, the big draw for this place is the leather couches, but don't get too worked up over it. Also, since the screen is so big, it really pays to be close to the center. I've been stuck on the edges several times and had to sit at uncomfortable angles. It really pays to get there early or go to a non-crowded showing. The theater itself is gorgeous, and you can tell the owners put a lot of work into restoring it to glory. It certainly is a "destination" theater and has reasonable prices, but at the end of the day, it's still just a movie theater. If you don't get your hopes up too high, you won't be disappointed.

text: I found this restaurant heading over to a buddies house. It was honestly so unexpectedly charming that I had to go there. I went to my buddies first for a spell, and he told me all about it, he gave the food a "pretty good", but warned to sit in the back of the restaurant away from the stage. Why? Apparently droves of wistful, wanna-be somebody, songwriters go there to croon their oaksy, rural journal entries to song. Not that it's a bad thing, he assured me. It just didn't go well for him when he went there once for a discrete meal, and was constantly hassled to engage in banter by a performer onstage, who wasn't very entertaining to begin with. Nightmare of a setting in that respect. I don't think the owner would have it any other way though. The setting is friendly with kind of a western-y vibe, serving seafood and Cajun specialties at fairly reasonable prices, really many items I have tried were very good. The highlight for me personally was the Crab Bisque, it was amazing, fresh, reasonably priced, real Crab. Bravo! Delicious! However the five times since I have been back it has been unavailable. I gave up, after realizing that, more than once, they were out of menu items all together, to the point of asking, "What do you actually have?". How can a restaurant be out of soup at 5:30 pm? All in all most Cajun places I have been to have been unoriginal, uninspired, and for the most part a ripoff for a plate of beans and rice, with a few slices of sausage. Ri'chard's is much better than this, for being able to raise itself murkily from the depths of an entire cuisine that is marketed solely on burnt Cajun seasoning, to the corn syrup clogged taste buds of the American public. Overall it's a friendly atmosphere, but problems occur and these problems effects the level of cuisine and service. I just don't think the owner is really into running a restaurant as much as he is into some grand aquarian episode onstage, jammin'. I personally was subjected to about 15 minutes of harmonica playing because the owner decided to jump onstage. That's great, be a showman, but at the same time give one of you other employees the capabilities of ringing customers out. The five notes played over, and over may have evoked angels in his reality. But not ours, or the other people waiting to leave. We all just wanted to be on with our plans, thanks for the lesson in all things that are crappy about grass roots music scenes. Go there and hope they are having a good day, it will be worth it sooner or later. Final Thought: When you buy your dessert's at grocery stores you may want to at least keep the packaging away from the counter. It's a poor reflection of your kitchens abilities. From Ri'chard's Website: this nails it on the head. Ingredients: 30 measures of great songs (crispy original style) 3 tons of talent (well shaken and marinaded) 10 gallons of supreme filler such as gumbo, jambalaya, shrimp, crawfish ... whatevers good. a yatch of rice Many handfulls of fun loving people A smattering of caring staff Served in laid back party atmosphere Method: Stir up everything together (add zydeco if desired) in a small town north of Nashville and watch it cook!

text: Powelton manages a bunch of houses and apartments in University City. I get the impression that they do most of their business with Drexel and Penn students. The claims I'll make about the business are based strictly on my experience as a renter in one of their 43rd Street row-homes, when I was a senior in college -- I can't really make broader claims about the company as a whole. Anyway. My roommate and I should have seen it coming. We were able to move in early because, for reasons we didn't understand at the time, the people before us anxiously wanted to get out. The place looked great when we went to the open house, but when we moved in a few weeks later, all the imperfections on the walls and floor were dreadfully exposed -- and unlike the crafty girls who'd lived there before us, my roommate and I didn't have the know-how to cover up all these eye sores. Nor did the realtor ever make an attempt to fix these things for us as, I believe, the contract suggested they would. That year, 2005, Winter came early and my poorly insulated bedroom on the third floor of the house turned frigid -- literally, it was dangerously cold, the sort of cold that the homeless flee to heated shelters to avoid. I would cover myself in three or four layers of blankets to go to sleep, and I'd still wake up freezing in the middle of the night. And my roommate and I must have called Powelton's central office ten times to ask them to have the heat turned on. I think, after a long time trying, we went to the office ourselves to demand that they send someone out immediately, and, finally, it got done. The problem with the heat in the building was, there was no way to control it; it was standardized for the whole house. And since heat rises, our third floor apartment became sauna-Esq. (But, okay, that was just the reality of the building: not really Powelton's fault.) And then there was the problem with the front door. The old locks got jammed one day, and I found myself locked out of my own apartment. I had to scream for the guys on the second floor to let me in. We called Powelton to fix the doors, but they never came. Two weeks later, the same thing happened again. Then we went to the office to complain and, finally, after more waiting they came. So, yes, the service sucked. Across the board. At one point, my roommate and I suggested that we ought to get a rent free month in exchange for our troubles, and we were, essentially, laughed at. Ha! But look, I didn't have a terrible experience in that apartment. The guys across the street threw these incredible retro-funk parties -- where the hell were those guys from? -- and, I remember, there was this really cool girl named Vicky who lived with them who could roll her own cigarettes in like 3 seconds flat. And the parties my roommate and I had in that place, shit, I think they were memorable. But, then again, we always laid out the change for good bear, not, ya know, Pabst. But we were thrilled to get out of there. In Spring, just before my graduation, the realtor started bringing new potential renters through the place. (I was mainly working on my thesis then, not getting out much, and he would sometimes surprise me with people when I was sitting at my computer in my underpants.) I never had the chutzpa to tell those kids about my experience, not there, not in front of the realtor. But I'm telling you, so I guess I am, in some way, maintaining justice in this world.

text: The Apple Store in Cherry Hill Mall. I would recommend the Sagemore branch over the Cherry Hill Mall branch. I live in Philadelphia and have been a Mac customer for 8 to 10 years. My experience at Cherry Hill Mall almost made me loose faith in the company and in all that Apple stood for in my eyes. The architecture and store layout was the same and consistent with other stores I've visited in the past but it lacked the same appeal. The Cherry Hill store was a mess, the familiar greeter to check you in was not there or was too busy working with other customers and the computers for the children were not functioning correctly not to mention the long lines of people waiting to talk to a Genius about malfunctioning machines. When I arrived with my family I set my son up on a computer but they didn't work. I waited for the greeter to check me in but none came. When I explained that I was in the store but was not able to get myself checked in there was no real attempt to rectify the situation but merely offered to rebook a reservation another day. After explaining that I lived in Philadelphia and could not get to New Jersey again I was told that another reservation could not be made until after 9:00pm which would have not been good for my family who needed to meet our bedtime rituals. I had already diagnosed my problem with my Iphone and I knew what the technicians would have said anyway I was merely following the protocol set by Apple Care Protection. Finally after talking for 20 minutes to the new guy I was told about a store 15 minutes away at Sagemore which I learned was the original Apple Store in that area. I was disappointed that they weren't able to accommodate me at the Cherry Hill store and that they didn't advise me about the other store close by but I reluctantly went to take care of the situation. At Sagemore I recieved the customer service I was accustomed to and the Genius Jon even explained more about the Iphone which was a welcomed conversation from what had happened at Cherry Hill. He was very knowledgeable and understanding about the situation at Cherry Hill. I commend his professionalism and the whole store functioned well including working computers for the kids. I asked about how to give feedback for the store and he immediately emailed me the survey which was much appreciated. Needless to say I am still a little wary of the accessibility that I once thought was important to the company. Iphone's are widely popular in Philadelphia but ATT can't service any of us. Springboard media are licensed to carry Apple but are still not sufficient in dealing with problems. Philadelphia desperately needs an Apple Store which has been rumored about for years but to no avail. ATT needs to be able to serve their Iphone customers, and when IPad comes out we would all benefit with a store handy to help us with whatever may happen.

text: 2.5 stars. I really wanted to like this place, but damnit, they failed. Not awful but not worthy of the current 4.5 star rating. And the food was meh for being a New Orleans southern restaurant. Here's what we had: App: crawfish etoufee - very tasty, no complaints about this except the price ($7 for a little cup!) Soup: Gumbo - this was okay but they got the gumbo's mixed up and gave me the chicken one instead of the seafood one Main: bf had "A Taste of Soul" Platter - Filé Gumbo, Red Beans & Rice, Jambalaya, Greens, Fried Chicken, Catfish Strips, and Bread Pudding, collard greens, while I had: Stuffed Bell Pepper - A green bell pepper stuffed with ground beef, shrimp, spices, and seasonings, baked and topped with our light home-style brown gravy, with red beans/rice, and mac/cheese shared the bread pudding for dessert BF really enjoyed his entree, while I found everything about mine to be lacking. BF's was good because all the fried seafood was low in fattiness, had a nice cornmeal crust and was light on oil. Mine sucked because the stuffing in the bell pepper was just whatever, and the mac and cheese was embarrassing - it had the texture of being reheated leftovers (overly mushy noodles and hard cheese) and tasted like almost nothing, box kraft is better. And it was not hot like the bell pepper. The cornbread was not warm either so I didn't get to enjoy any nice crust on top. Bread pudding dessert was hot and delicious, though it had nuts so it automatically became all mine. This was the best part of the meal. Beyond the food being less than impressive, at least my dish, the service was pretty lacking. It took a looong time for a server to get to us, while a neighboring party sat down later, ordered and received their food before us. Another neighboring party had super crappy service too, and even asked for a comment card, and of course did not get one. They could have walked out and not paid, given that they had to actually flag someone else down and ask them to please take their money so they could go, those words literally. So, I say there is a lot of room for improvement here.
label: NEG

text: Max Brenners is great... and an excellent alternative to not eating chocolate. We got the asian salad and the southwestern caesers salad. Maybe they were on the pricier end for the amount of salad you get, but not offensively overpriced. Of the two I'd recommend the asian salad... the soba noodles and chicken really make it flavorful. But who goes to a chocolate restaurant and doesn't eat chocolate? We split a 'Golden Heart'... chocolate cake with chocolate on the inside, hot caramel drizzled on the plate, and bananas in toffee sauce. We also ordered a scoop of vanilla ice cream with it. Over all it was way more good than bad. I mean for $13 the little slice of cake better be good... The chocolate is rich, hot and decadent. The cake was nice and warm, and complimented by the vanilla ice cream nicely. A side note, not sure where they got their ice cream from, but it's not run of the mill... it's very good. This was an amazing dessert. Some negatives to ponder... the caramel sauce was almost impossible to get out of this stupid little 'beaker' they served it in. Also the cake took around 20 minutes to be served. This was during a very uncrowded lunch time. Maybe they were back there baking the cake, or running around Philly trying to find ice cream or something... but it seemed unreasonably long to wait. All in all it's a little pricy for what you get... but you are getting something that will make you roll your eyes into the back of your head. I'd say skip the food and go straight for dessert. Definitely worth a visit.

text: National Mechanics is by far my favorite bar in Philadelphia. I live in the Art Museum area and I would prefer to trek all the way to Old City than hang out in my own neck of the woods. Paul, Lauren, Drew and the gang ROCK, HARDCORE. Ignore that one review about Drew. I appreciate the fact that "NAT MECS" does not feel the need to have PBR to generate a crowd. Come to Mechanics if you are a beer person. Mechanics celebrates the local brews with Yards and PBC on tap. It's also a place that barely advertises and is always full at night. You can plan your whole week here! Well, I do. Monday, when open, lunch with my old city buddies. Tuesday, if you feel up to it, karaoke night! Wednesday, hang out with John and get a team together for PUB QUIZ. Thursday, just hang the !@#$ out! Friday, sometimes SIDESHOW, most of the time, a great place to meet and hang! It's a favorite for all of the historical organizations like the National Park Service and Once Upon A Nation staff. Saturday, another hangout night if you get there a little early. The place fills up fast! Sunday, start your day with an amazing brunch menu. I am a hung fan of the french toast! Go somewhere else for the rest of the day, then come back around 9 and play Wii on the big screen! if National Mechanics opened a WAWA and a little Coffee Bar, I would not need to go anywhere else! Oh, and a little bookstore with a small selection of high-end adult magazines...hehe. In 2008, Once Upon A Nation made National Mechanics the first stop on the Tippler's Tour which runs every Thursday from April through October! Oh! I forgot to mention, the place has WI-FI!!! And it's Free!!! All you haters need to stop hatin on Nat Mecs! Some girl got her feelings hurt because Drew didn't think she was sexier than his hot, hot, hot girlfriend, so service was bad...haha! Makes "Mecs, YOURS!"

text: Worst service I have ever experienced. I brought my scooter here to have the rear tire changed after driving over a nail. My brother and I loaded the scooter into his van and pulled up right in front of the shop to unload it. We were obviously struggling trying to keep the rear doors open and get the bike on the ground. I noticed a guy leaning against the store and watching us, and he offered no help, but I figured he's just a random inconsiderate bystander. Not the case. Once I entered the shop, I discovered it is the OWNER of the scooter shop. Seriously? I am struggling to unload a scooter in front of you and you can't even hold the door for me? It was so difficult just to get it there that I didn't have much of a choice in whether to leave it there or not. I was told the tire was in stock and they would probably get to it that day. 4 days of unreturned phone calls later, they told me they had to order the tire. 2 WEEKS later, they had managed to change the back tire. Unfortunately, this is not the end of the story. I've ridden the scooter three times since getting it back and it is getting progressively worse to the point where I am afraid to even ride it back to the shop. It is making a rubbing and clunking sound (coming from the rear tire) and when the rear brake is applied it makes a horrible grinding sound. The owner told me the following: 1. They can't even look at it for a couple of weeks. 2. He doubts it is because of something they did. 3. "They test drive all the scooters after changing a tire." This is absolutely not true because when I picked the bike up, they told me it needed a new battery because they couldn't get it to start. The kill switch was on. I turned it off and started the bike on the first try. This means they either don't know their stuff or they were trying to con me into buying a battery from them. 4. "I'm not going to argue this with you over the phone" 5. "Don't take this the wrong way, but a lot of people need their bikes fixed" Lastly, while I waited for an hour to pick up my bike, I heard the employees arguing with several people over the phone and telling them "We have a policy not to discuss prices over the phone." We looked at the menu a bit, and decided to go with the crispy crab empanadas, as well as a Schlafly pumpkin ale for me (woo!) and a whiskey and coke for the boy. The empanadas were not good. The breading tasted a lot like a pot pie, and the filling tasted like tuna, not crab. Hmm. The mango salsa that accompanied the appetizer was flavorless. I was hoping to have better luck with the entree. I went with the jerk chicken sandwich with french fries. The sandwich was just okay. Very cheesy, but not very...jerk-y? Isn't jerk seasoning supposed to be a bit spicy? This wasn't. It wasn't too flavorful either, to be honest. The kaiser roll that the meat came on was just sad. The whole thing was just bland. The seasoned fries were terrific, though! I saw that they had bread pudding on the dessert menu, so OF COURSE I had to try that! It came out piping hot and covered in a bourbon sauce. This was probably the best part of the meal. It was soft, gooey, and tasted just like french toast. A+! The service was friendly, but slow. It seemed like that was ONE waitress taking care of the entire restaurant. Are they always this slow, or was it just an unusually busy night? I don't know. She was friendly, so I'm not going to complain too much. I'm glad we had a Groupon so we could try this place. Sadly, I seriously doubt we'll be back. Maybe for drinks (my pumpkin ale was delish, as was Andy's Whiskey and coke!), but definitely not for food. Save your money. Go elsewhere.

text: Frankie's place is probably the best place for Italian food done to perfection on the Main Line. Even though the name of the place is Fellini Cafe, it is not part of a chain, as stated by a previous reviewer although the name may have originally been associated. Frankie's food is nothing like the other places (which I have tried). I have probably have been there over 20 times and honestly have not had a bad meal. It's BYOB and we usually bring a red and white wine so we can choose based upon what the evening specials are. One of our off menu favorites is the roasted pork chop with broccoli rabe and roasted potatoes. The Veal Milanese with hot and sweet peppers never disappoints. Classic standbys of gnocchi and spaghetti with bolognese sauce work well every time; the meatballs are the third best I have ever had (my wife makes the best, my mother-in-law, the second best). The fish dishes are delicious and someone in the group always orders the mussels with red sauce, which is a definite pleaser. After a very satisfying dinner, be sure to enjoy one of the excellent desserts. The cannoli are hand filled when you place your order (so no getting soggy during the day) and Frankie's pizelle-ice cream sandwich with home-made gelati (three types, the pistachio is incredible) with fresh made caramel sauce (Frankie makes it himself when you order) has you licking the plate clean. Aside from the great food, the service is always personal and Frankie comes out to greet everyone - all feel like regulars and the wait staff are quick to respond to special requests. The place is tight - very much European in its nature (if you don't like people, don't come) - but everyone is friendly and ready to let you know how much they like what they are eating (my wife is always asking about something new that someone else has ordered). Unfortunately, we've had to move far enough away that getting over is a very very long drive, but whenever we are in town, we always stop in for a bite to eat.

text: FedEx Kinko's is the half-wit child of two independently successful and respectable parent companies. You can stand there for five minutes and no one will look your way. Then if you say something like, "Hi, I need some help," they just look up at you like you're a vagrant in need of something hot to drink on a cold day. I think in the break room they have three things on their wall: the sign that lectures about sexual harassment, the sign that posts the legal minimum wage, and a symbol that says "Customer Service" with a red slash through it right next to the No Smoking placard. This abominable service has happened four times so far. If this happens to you in the future, take it personally and report it to the manager. Then tell them off and leave. I've never been as disgruntled a customer as when I've been in this store. It makes you long for the days of personalized service and attention to detail. If you can go to a real UPS or FedEx store, do it.

text: Flowing Well is an 18-acre oasis that sits on the north side of 116th Street, midway between the center of Carmel and the center of Fishers. This park is something of a well-kept secret (not as much so if you live in the immediate vicinity), which is unfortunate because it is so peaceful and shady here. One thing I like about this park is that it has retained much of the mature tree growth rather than having been cleared to make playgrounds, prairies and the like. On a hot day, this is still a nice place to be outside. The park offers fishing, picnic shelters and walking trails - some of the trail path is even paved, making it accessible to just about anybody. However, the thing that makes this park truly unique among the Carmel-Clay Parks & Recreation family is the flowing well for which it is named. A flowing artesian well is the highlight here and people come from miles around to fill jugs and bottles with the cool, refreshing water that bubbles up from an aquifer below the park grounds. The well was actually discovered by accident during a natural gas drilling expedition in the early 1900s. Rather than gas, the crew found the underground aquifer, which apparently created a small geyser when it was tapped into. The result all these years later: Carmel's very own public flowing well. One of the best ways to enjoy this park is to take your empty water bottle with you, fill it up at the well - which is conveniently situated at the park's entrance - and then take a hike on the trails. You'll enjoy beautiful foliage, flowers and Cool Creek along the way, as well as, that delicious FREE spring water! BTW: while dogs are welcome at the park - on a leash of course - they may not drink directly from the flowing well spigots so be sure to bring a small tupperware or other water dish for your four-legged companion :-)

The quoted 15 to 20 minutes for a table inside was actually less than 5 minutes. I would not discourage anyone from eating here, and yes, I'm sure we will be back. This is a small, locally owned chain that recently expanded to include 6 locations across the Tampa Bay area. I hate to say this, but every time enterprises like this expand there seems to be less emphasis on the quality of the food and more on the location and trendiness of the establishment. text: Estia appears to garner high praise and enthusiastic endorsements from many of its patrons; why, however, is not obvious to me. My wife and I (in town for a getaway weekend) came here at the recommendation of our hotel concierge. His two prior suggestions had been spot-on, but he missed the boat with this one. Estia is pretty much like every other Greek restaurant you've ever been to. A bit more deliberately upscale, perhaps, but with the same cacaphonous and slightly chaotic ambience. There's nothing wrong with that - but there's nothing special about it either. Don't come here expecting an evening of elegant dining. The food was - okay. I will happily acknowledge that my lamb chops were tasty and tender, that we enjoyed the hummus and bread, and the calamari appetizer was light and tender. The menu was stock Greek fare, however; the romaine and country salads were unremarkable, and the wine list was too deliberately confined to Greek vintages. Our principal disappointment was the service. The most suitable adjective might be "perfunctory". The waitstaff seemd to be phoning it in - coming to take our order, then to take our empty plates, and finally to deliver the check. We saw far more of the fellow who refilled our water glasses (attentively) then we ever did of our actual waiter. And when the check did come, delivered by a woman whom we had not theretofore seen, she deposited it on our table without even breaking stride, in a practiced and fluid movement that reminded me of nothing so much as a body being rolled out the door of a moving car. Look, it wasn't awful. I've had much worse experiences. (In a way I wish this had been one of them, so that I would at least have the pleasure of telling and re-telling the story.) It was just utterly, completely, uninspiring, and far short of the expectations that we'd taken into the place. If you like Greek / Mediterranean food, and are don't mind feeling a bit like you're just another of the evening's couple hundred customers, then it's fine. But if you're looking for something fresh, a new experience or a special night out, there are *lots* of better choices in town.

Isaac had the Pork Chops Siciliano- homemade vinegar peppers over deliciously large grilled center-cut pork chops. Served with oven-roasted potatoes and roasted vegetables. Not-so-good. All the doctoring in the world couldn't make his food better. The pork was over cooked and the veggies were undercooked. But he Bar:is a man who will eat anything, so he made due. text: I will NEVER go back to Cliff's, after experiencing the most unprofessional service ever. I wouldn't even give it one star. I recently brought in a sandal for repair. The man working there was very friendly and promised the repair would be done within 3 days. I paid the cost of the repair upfront, faithful that the repair would be done in a timely manner. I also left the other shoe, which was in perfect condition, with him, as he had asked to use it for reference on the shoe's construction. When I returned to pick up on the date he had promised, I arrived to find he was not there. Someone else carelessly told me to come back after the weekend. When I returned on Monday, I was informed that it was not ready and to come back tomorrow. When I came a third time, I was told it was, again, not ready, and the man complained about being swamped with work over the weekend and lamented about how he had so much to do and was there by himself. If I returned at 5 pm, he'd have it. I came back at 5 pm, the 4th time I'd come to pick it up, and he said that the shoes were not there, but at another location. If I came the next day, he'd have it. When I went FOR THE FIFTH TIME to pick up my shoes, he looked at me woefully and told me "that there was a problem." He had fixed my shoe, finally, BUT HAD LOST THE OTHER ONE. The situation was beyond ludicrous. Instead of completely owning up to his mistake and incompetence, he said that "no one was perfect" and blamed the shoe itself, saying that it was a little shoe and easy to lose track of. I am livid. Not only was my repair not done in a timely fashion, but he lost the match to the shoe, making the repair to the one shoe useless. It doesn't matter if I have the shoe fixed if I don't have the other one to match it. He gave me a refund on the repair, but it doesn't come close to amounting to the cost of the shoes. He's been "looking" for the shoe for a few days now, and he hasn't found it. It's only fair that he refund me the cost of the pair, since I've gone through all this extra trouble on a simple repair. So far, nothing. I'm disappointed that such a long-standing business could be so unprofessional and inconsiderate about the needs and priorities of its consumers. Even if they do find the shoe, I will never go back, and I would HIGHLY DISCOURAGE anyone considering going there. Customers are a privilege, and if a shoe repair place is going to be so careless with both shoes and business, they don't deserve patronage.

text: This place used to be better - I've been going to Nature's Food Patch for several years, its right down the street from my work and incredibly convenient. Unfortunately I've seen the store slowly declining in its quality and with the competition that has opened across the bay (Wild Oats and soon the Publix Greenwise marketplace) I find my visits less and less frequent. While I try to support the smaller, longer standing institutions even when the competition is priced less, I'm just repeatedly dissapointed with the direction this place has headed. I'm a vegan so shopping at a natural food store is pretty much a requirement to a well-rounded cupboard. Their grocery section is very adequate and actually priced quite reasonably when compared to other small natural food stores or even the big chains. I have, however, run into a frequent problem of purchasing vegan 'dairy' items and find that they are spoiled. This has happened to me on several occasions when purchasing fake cheese products, many of which were not even close to their expiration date, which leads me to believe that they may be improperly storing some of the food items that require refrigeration. For this reason I only buy dry good from them now. As for the deli, they made several improvements over the past few months but the quality and convenience has actually declined. To start off with the good, they do now have a hot food section which is great for lunch. No more bringing back cold lunches or having to reheat your meals in the company microwave! Also, they've expanded their racks to provide prepackaged foods from the deli cases including their pasta salads, tofu, and even sandwiches and wraps. Unfortunately, when they expanded the cases they did away with the convenient name tags that said whether or not items were Omnivore, Vegetarian, or Vegan. So now you have to ask the assistant behind the counter and the majority of the time wait while they scan the ingredients and give a not-so-helpful reply of, 'I think its vegan?" And while the prepackaged food is convenient so you do not have to stand in line... its been my recent experiences that prepared food in the deli has been suffering from quality controls that has lead to poor taste or even foreign objects in my wraps. Lastly, as someone whose been eating at the deli for several years, it would be nice if they brought in some new dishes for variety. To their credit, whenever I've had problems they've been very polite and offered to either exchange the item or offered me store credit. They seem sincere about improving the conditions but I see little change from visit to visit. When I shop here its for convenience and only for dry goods. Otherwise, I make a trip once or twice a month to Wild Oats and pickup a stockpile of my vegan essentials.
label: NEG

text: there are literally thousands upon thousands of reasons why Pat's is a superior steak establishment to Geno's, which are in no way limited to the superiority of the steaks themselves. yes, you will always eat a better cheesesteak at Pat's... but let us examine some of the non-culinary reasons why Geno's does not deserve your business or mine: 1. the facade -- let's be honest. Geno's is an aesthetic embarassment. while Pat's scores points with an understated and humble exterior, Geno's has always tried to compensate for their inferior product by dressing the whole place up in a vomit-inducing sea of neon lights. take a note, Geno: the lights only illuminate your desperation. 2. the menu -- Geno's is the only place I have ever heard of (outside of the cafeteria in our fair halls of congress, that is) that ever replaced their "french fries" with "freedom fries". that's right. they call them freedom fries. yeeee-ikes. 3. the xenophobia -- Notoriously opposed to the post-italian immigrants in south philly, and probably pissed at the five or six french tourists who visit philadelphia a year, the window at Geno's features a delightful little sign which states "this is AMERICA please speak ENGLISH when ordering" followed by a sign stating "Management Reserves the Right to Refuse Service". and if you think the message in sign 1 has never intersected with the policy in sign 2, think again. what a fine ambassador to our city you are, Genie-boy! 4. the plaque -- underneath the window is a plaque hung in honor of fallen police officer Daniel Faulkner. for non-delphians, this name might not mean much, but he is the victim in our city's highest-profile and most hot-button murder case. (i won't go into the details, but if you want to know more about what this is all about, you'll find plenty of info when you google "Mumia".) my issue is not that they honor the memory of this police officer, which i think is perfectly appropriate if done respectfully. what seems kind of messed up is the fact that the plaque gives equal time to the officer's accused murderer: it just seems really inappropriate, and i can't imagine it would make any friends or family of officer faulkner feel very good if they have to be reminded of the murderer's name every time they see the plaque. i don't mean to focus too heavily on this cheesesteakery's politics, but in being so flagrant about it they clearly invite the scrutiny. the bottom line is this: Pat's is just a better steak, and if it's too hard for you to make up your mind based on the variables of taste, texture, size, and service... there are plenty of other factors you can use to justify your decision. Perhaps the sign on Pat's window says it best --- "Don't eat a Mis-steak"

text: Rosepepper - the East Nashville Mexican staple. I've been hearing about Rospepper for years, especially about their award winning margarita. That's unfortunately the only thing that was really award-winning about my experience with Rosepepper. I'll start at the beginning: Chips and salsa came out. Chips were crisp and fresh. An assortment of three salsas came out, mild, verde, and "hot", the "hot" being quite a good salsa. (Rosepepper's explanation of my criticizing the unspicy "hot" sauce might be that their focus is on Sonora-style Mexican cuisine, which is in nature not spicy. Eh, whatever.) Really, it was maybe the best thing I ate. The verde salsa was syrupy and extremely mild, and maybe too sweet. And the mild salsa - could hardly pass as salsa. It was tomato paste with a few herbs and spices. We had a casa margarita and a frozen peach margarita. These margaritas are HARDCORE. Lots of alcohol. They're well made and homemade. However, if you're lookin' for a real sweet concoction, I'd hit Cantina Laredo first. And ladies go on Ladies Night Thursdays when the margaritas are $6. We had the fish tacos and a combination plate including a bean chimichanga and chicken taco. Chimiganga was a cute burrito-sized fried pocket filled with yummy beans and topped with a Buffalo cheese sauce. Yummy, it's hard to go wrong with an item like this - especially for me, because I love beans. I know it sounds funny, but I really do. The chicken taco was really bland. Flavorless! Well cooked and well, but totally without any character. Fish tacos were well battered, and accompanied by a tangy mayo sauce. Did I mention tangy?? This may be the most amusing part of my meal. The combination platter was accompanied by "lime veggies". Sounds like an over-complimentary description for what came out on the plate, which was clearly raw carrots, cucumber, and celery. Uh, nice try. You know, it's a cool place with a varied menu. I know it's a really hip hang, any restaurant with the cheapest margarita priced at $8 would be. But honestly from my experience tonight, I wouldn't come here again. The service was plenty fine and the setting was fine, but the food just wasn't good enough.

text: It has to be difficult to own a restaurant that sits in the looming shadow of the infamous Venice Cafe. Not that, at the end of the day, Venice is something so special that you can't possibly coincide with them, but imagine how difficult it would be to get people to notice your brand new taupe-colored siding if your next door neighbor had decorated their house in a glittery mosaic of jazz hands and rainbows. Now yes, Frazer's may not be the kind of place where you can pay for a sandwich with a song, but honestly I'm not really one to sing in public anyway. Their atmosphere is formal enough to match their amazing food but not too stuffy so that you feel you have to dress up or can't relax. Their servers are also friendly and knowledgeable and I have found them to be very helpful when deciding what to order. It's nice to have someone who can explain the specials in an authoritative way without talking over your head or being pushy with the up-sell. On a recent trip to Frazer's, we brought an out-of-town guest there for the first time. The goal was to kick back, have a few drinks and have a delicious but "normal" meal. We absolutely accomplished this goal at Frazer's. For starters we had the cheese plate and the chorizo stuffed dates. Both dishes were very flavorful and a great start to the meal. Among the three of us at the table our order consisted of only items from the special's board. I personally had the sweet potato enchiladas and holy crap they were good! You will not hear me say that often about a vegetarian item but I will definitely have those again. Ok, now let me go back to the chorizo stuffed dates... I order this dish every single time that I go to Frazer's and I don't see me changing this pattern anytime soon. Frazer and his crew are doing some amazing things here with, to be quite honest, a food item that I have long since avoided, the date. You get 4 of what looks like a small meatball, in a spicy tomato sauce. Not having seen how they make these, I won't even begin to act like I know how they're prepared but let me sum it up for you: they take a ball full of MAGIC and wrap it in a strip of BACON. Yes, I said it, BACON! Simultaneously you taste a little spicy, from the chorizo, sweet, from the date, salty from the bacon, and acidic from the tomato sauce, in what is an incredibly delicate balance of awesome flavors. I could honestly go on about the stuffed dates for hours but all I really need to say is get off your butt, trek out in the snow (it's worth it) and get yourself and order of your own. Now! Oh yeah, they have beers and cool stuff like that too. Be sure to get your drink on while you're at it. Bacon!

text: How can I put a star review on a major hospital. The stars really depend on different things. I know the ER really well b/c I volunteered there for 3 years. This is the ER to hit if you have a non-trauma emergency. However, I have learned that it is best to avoid the ER if you can and see your regular doctor instead. Of course, if you have abdominal pain or its late at night, you can't avoid a trip to the ER. PA Hospital's ER has shorter waits than HUP or Jefferson. I do know that, but I also know people get upset with the waits that can be long. I have some tips for the ER. 1) If possible, show up in the off hours, morning, early afternoon or late at night. Showing up at 5 pm is going to suck. 2) Bring a friend to keep you company and advocate for you. 3) They have food in the ER, but won't let you eat until all the tests are done. Get ready to be hungry. Most of the ER rooms have tv's and there is access to bathrooms. They have phones in most of the rooms, but won't yell at you if you sneak a cell phone call or two. You can get a cab once you leave, but you need to call the cab yourself. Ok, review of ER done... I did stay in PA Hospital recently. No complaints about the stay. Nice place except insurance didn't pay for it. PA Hospital didn't fight for me to be there. It was kind of a debacle. I needed care. I had insurance, but we ended up paying out of pocket. So basically I was screwed by both PA Hospital and the insurance company. I tried to fight it, but it was too hard. I gave up.
label: NEG

text: This thrift store is a great find! You walk in, and have to first get over the sight of tons of stuffed animal heads on the walls of the place, but after that you find a plethora of great items for your home. The store is huge, they have room after room of all kinds of antique and new furniture and housewares. Apparently, they buy out all of the items from houses and then sell them for cheap. My roommate and I got 2 mattresses (no box spring), an old desk, and a leather chair for 230 bucks! It was quite the deal. The employees there are extremely friendly and willing to make a deal on the furniture you want. If you are in need of some furniture and want to buy it cheap, check out this place first!

text: Had guests visiting this weekend and decided to give Monk's a try. They have a large beer selection and a decent sized menu. I ordered a burger and it was really good. text: For me, the burger hierachy goes In-n-Out -- The Habit -- Five Guys (East Coast Chain) -- All other Chains. This is a very solid burger, and again, I'm a big supporter of local chains. The burger was cooked well and there were just the right amount of toppings. The only reason I prefer In-n-Out more is because I prefer "special sauce" (thousand island rather than mayo or ketchup) and I like toasted buns. However, what makes this a very close second is that the fries and onion rings are very good, and they have ranch dressing for you to dip them in. Yeah, not exactly a healthy meal but I don't eat out often (random tidbit: the chicken sandwich actually has more fat and calories than the burger though). Although all of the Habit's environments are fun, the outdoor seating and old pictures here make you feel like you're at an authentic burger shack. Just go to the light on Hollister and go around the back to find parking; turning into their narrow one-way driveway seems like a disaster waiting to happen.

text: These people who are so negative on Royal China probably eat at Fong's in Kenner, LA. Yeah the place is dingy but no one makes combination fried rice like this place. text: I write this from the living room at this very hotel, the only place with free wifi. The next paragraph will be my Cliff's Notes review for those wanting the short version (which is essentially, this place is a dump). More detail in following paragraphs. This place is a dump. They think that by adding some cheap but modern furniture downstairs and some Design Within Reach outdoor furniture, people will believe this is a high class hotel. It's really just an old building with small and very dirty rooms. If you are a reasonably clean person, you'll have a hard time with your room, as both rooms we had were quite dirty. It's a party place mostly for young gay men, so if you're looking for that you'll enjoy the social aspect. Don't be fooled by the photos - the pool is rinky dink and packed. The only cool thing is the Acura experience, which saves you a cab fare going to anyplace within 6 miles of the hotel (but won't pick you back up). More detail - make sure they give you the right room. We paid for a Spectacular room, but first were put into a standard room, which we didn't know until we had to have the housekeeping supervisor up to see how dirty the room was (dusty, stopper out of the sink because it had drainage problems, etc.). We finally repacked and got to our "Spectacular room", which is supposed to be spectacular because of the view - the side of a building. What is the non-spectacular view? At some point you have to get over it and get on with having a good time, which we did, but we would definitely not stay at this dirt hotel again. Not your typical W hotel.

Because, as we found, the food at Plate was either bland or just off. Baked brie with caramelized onions was sickly sweet and served with sesame crackers that were too hard and didn't really complement the cheese, house bread was pretty flavorless and the weird spread they served with it was just not tasty. Mussels in wine sauce were fine but i had to add salt. When we got the dessert menu, many of the items had annoyingly childish names--words like "fudgie wudgie." We ordered a peanut butter chocolate cake which didn't taste great and had way too much going on (rice crispy crust, drizzled with cheap chocolate and caramel sauces, doused with powdered sugar) Furthermore, the repetitive "trendy beats" playing were obnoxious, and the decor was trying too hard and definitely didn't cover up for the crappy food. Too expensive, obnoxious, and disappointing. either go somewhere where 12 dollar appetizers and 24 dollar entrees are justified, or find someplace less pretentious, lower priced, and still delicious.

text: No joke, this place is what I will miss about New Orleans. (We're moving, not the restaurant.) Gosh, we're regulars here for the past 2 years and EVERYTHING is worth trying. I am not going into details about what I ordered..etc. because you will be satisfied. Whatever you order, add plantains and spinach if it doesn't come with your dish. Full of spices, stew-like quality to it and always comforting. Family owned; we like to support local business. Great place for conversations and first timers. We live within walking distance so I don't know how parking would be like but I can certainly see that it may be a while for you to find a place to park your car w/o being ticketed afterwards- it is the FQ. Normally, Bennachin's has a table for you if it's a party of 4 or less but anything more, call and make reservations. Like Amada, I don't think I could go wrong with any order. The service was good, and our waiter was very personable. The place is dark and cozy, like Amada but I honestly only saw the place from the door to my table. So i can't speak for the rest of the place and have no idea how spacious or not it is. Amada is still my favorite, like the straight A's, good looking, plays 4 instruments, 5 sports, speaks 3 languages, and ivy league bound child. text: Metropolitan Bakery is my favorite bakery in Philly. The bread is incredible, especially their multigrain. They culture their starters instead of using commercial yeast and it makes a very big difference in the taste. They make the only sourdough I have ever liked, this is due to the natural cultures, which most modern bakeries won't even bother with. I can never finish a whole loaf, but their bread freezes and thaws well. Their sweets are also great, the chocolate cherry bread is rich without being too sweet. It is a nice treat for adults. Their croissants are amazing as well, they have a big of delicious dark chocolate in the center. Their scones are bread-like but wonderfully flavored. I love their french berry roll, each one is beautiful and full of fruit (I especially like it when they use figs, but what you get varies by what's in season). It isn't cheap, but the owners really know what they are doing. Places that put this much time and effort into producing something as simple as bread are few and far between.
label: POS

Maybe it's just my opion of taste or something like that. But one of my family members said it was not that great and he eats alot! IYou can try this place but if your like me, you won't like it!

text: Delightful interpretation of latin-asian fusion. Another one of Jose Garces restaurants had to be visited by me, since overall I like his concepts in general. Chifa is another great restaurant on his list. It wasn't hard to find the place near 7th and Chestnut, and parking was a breeze since there is a lot right next door. It's sorta dark when you walk in at first, but once you walk back and see the color scheme and lighting and the seating, you get it, and like it. Very soothing and modern, not ultra modern but cool. There was a good amount of seating, open tables and booths. Scanning the menu, there was a mix, ceviches, salads, seafood, meats. There was a tasting menu with three tiers, which we chose from. The food was excellent, highlights were the ceviche which we had to start. This was fresh and lots of flavors which all complimented each other. The chicken dish we had was again great, well seasoned and not sure if it was roasted or grilled but it was well cooked and plentiful. My favorite was the pork belly buns. I don't know what it is but pork belly and I are best friends. The buns were bite sized and the pork was excellent, enough fat and meat and in good proportions. The hoisin glaze gave it a different but good taste. Service was great, our waiter was very knowledgeable about the menu and made good recommendations on drinks and deserts, and explained the menu well. At first while being served our first dish, we were sort of overwhelmed at the pace which things were being brought out, but then it made sense. The majority of the lighter dishes, like salads and ceviche came out first and there was a pause for a few minutes and then came the meats and fish. The tasting menu was a good value seeing that for three people we had left overs on most dishes, especially the chicken and steak. So that was well worth it. I recommend it if its your first time there!
label: POS

text: Oh. My. Goodness. Why haven't I dined here sooner? Jesus, I've truly been missing out on super yummy food. I could live without all the snobby yuppies that turned around and stared at us when we walk in the door, but that happens at a lot of places. The woman at the table next to us kept staring at Mike O., I know he has crazy hair and looks like a cave man, but we like to eat good food too. I just wonder isn't their conversation good enough to not notice me and my tattoos? And what about the food? The food is so good I'd probably wouldn't notice if someone was getting the heimlich maneuver right next to me. It's that good! We opted for the 3 courses for $40. I started with the fall salad and Mike O. went with the vitello tonnato. I have four words for you: bone marrow is delicious! I have to admit his was f-ing phenomenal and I wish I would have noticed it on the menu. I was disappointed with mine in comparison. Salty goodness wins over veggies any day, no matter what, ever. Don't get me wrong, mine was good with goat cheese and veggies, but good lord above why didn't I notice it in the menu? For our entree we split the 16 oz rib-eye with the $10 upcharge. So worth it! The sauce was amazing and the meat tender and cooked medium. I'm pretty sure I melted into my seat for a minute. The rib-eye was served with potato puree and an arugula salad. All had amazing texture and went perfect together. For dessert we split a cheese plate (another upcharge) and the liquid chocolate cake. The cheese plate had three cheeses, a cranberry paste, spicy roasted nuts and bread. I enjoyed all of it, a lot. The liquid chocolate cake was pretty amazing and served along side with chocolate ice cream. Chocolate and cheese = satisfied. I ordered the signature drink the "Last Word". It was good, but I wished I had ordered wine instead. For me it just would have went better with the meal. I was offered the drink straight up or on the rocks. Cool. I'm an on the rocks kind of girl and guess what? Another upcharge for ice! I get the upcharge for the other options, but for ice, really? I'll admit the cubes were perfect and square, but for real the drink was $9, you can't put ice in for free? I upcharged everything else I could so I'm not being cheap. I didn't come here thinking I wasn't going to drop $150, but for some reason that frosted my cake. Gerard, for the love of god why are you charging for ice? If there is some complicated process used to make the perfect cubes I might be able to let it go but as of right now I'm still a little peeved. Our server was nice and friendly but not overly friendly. She was attentive but to not too attentive. I liked her a lot. One of the other servers came over and chatted with me about tattoos which I thought was cool. Usually I get silly questions, but he was nice and made me feel comfortable, not like a freak as the patrons may have earlier in the evening. Niche is fantastic. I will dine here again. I wish I could afford to go here more often. I think I might be addicted to the vitello tonnato.

text: I would estimate that I've honestly dropped a couple thousand dollars at Flying Pie, so I feel well qualified to submit a review. Flying Pie unquestionably serves the finest pizza in Boise and about the best I've found anywhere. First and foremost, the pizza is absolutely delicious. I've learned that different pizzas appeal to different persons, so the fact that I like it is not necessarily determinative for you. The pizza is medium but crispy crust with lots and lots of very high-quality ingredients. The crust is half-way between thin-crust New York pizzas and deep dish Chicago pizzas. The ingredients are super quality and there are lots of them. Those are the key aspects of the superiority of a Flying Pie pizza. Also, the various crusts are yummy and the pizzas are always properly cooked to crispy (crust) but gooey (cheese) perfection. The pizzas are very creative and there is a wide variety. My favorites are the zambini (sausage and jalapenos), the Denver Pie (think a Denver omelet) and the mesquite chicken. While the pizza is not inexpensive, I believe that Flying Pie is a good value. So why only four stars rather than five?, you might ask. I'll tell you. It's two things. The restaurants are dumps in very undistinguished locations. Hanging out at the Flying Pie, either location, is like hanging out in your friend's basement in 1982. The owners invested $2,450 to outfit the spaces in 1982 and haven't put a penny in since. I'm all for a funky vibe, but this crosses over from funky vibe to junky dive. The price for the pizza is at the high end but the interiors are low quality, dark shops located next to a Salvation Army depot and trailer parks (State Street) and tattoo parlors (Fairview). My second beef is that the restaurant has an almost-juvenile self-congratulation streak. In their publications, menus, sign boards, and attitude, the restaurant is always telling the customer how incredibly awesome they are. We're awesome and have the best pizza! We're incredibly awesome and everyone loves our pizza! We're the best restaurant ever and our pizza is better than everybody else's!! Ok, I get it and I'm tired of it. I don't mind when my 8 year old tells me he's awesome, but after that it's a little embarrassing. It's especially annoying in light of the dumpy physical spaces. If you're so awesome, why don't you make your interiors pleasant? If you're so awesome, why don't you put a location downtown? it seems to me that the owners should focus a little less on self-congratulation and a little more on improving the customer experience, non-eating wise. All those things being said, i think the service is excellent; the spaces are clean; and given that many of the employees have worked there for a very very long time, it must be a good place to work.

text: Worst doctor experience EVER. If I could give negative stars, this would be it. Castelli (I don't even want to call him "Doctor") is the most arrogant and appalling human being I've ever had the misery of meeting. He's the head doctor of Womens Health Care Specialists, which is the office located here. I had been in to Dr. Philip Hirshman, who also works at this practice (and is amazing!). Long story short (walking the fine boundary here between TMI and trying to explain why you should avoid Castelli at all costs), I had a mysterious lump that I wanted checked out ASAP, and Dr. Hirshman was booked for the next few weeks. However, Castelli was free the next day. That probably should have been my first red flag. But the receptionist said that he's been practicing for over 20 years, so I agreed. I show up for my appointment, and wait in the waiting room for over an hour. Next, I'm shepherded into a room, where I'm told to undress, and then end up waiting another 20 minutes (with not even a magazine to amuse me). I was already annoyed at having waited so long, and it really was just downhill from there. Finally, Castelli walks in, no apologies or introductions. He smarms at me for about 30 seconds, making light of something I was stressed out about, took one look, said he couldn't tell what it, and prepared to end the appointment. At no point did Castelli take my history, ask if I was sexually active or if I'd ever had a pap, mention HPV or STDs (or any possible cause at all!), or give me any advice on what to do. At this point, I should mention that I have no qualms about asserting myself, and that I've been in the field of sexual health/women's health for over ten years, so I of course started asking totally reasonable questions, like, "What should I do? Is it going to go away? Can you test to see if it's anything I should be concerned about?" In response to each question, he kept on saying that he'd "addressed that already" (he had not) and that I should "do nothing" and keep progressing as normal. In other words, I should just wait it out and see if it gets worse or comes back. There was nothing I should do. Nothing at all. And this "advice" was given to me only after I specifically asked, because he definitely didn't offer up any of this "information" during his initial exam. I finally managed to get him to mention some treatment I could look into if the bumps came back, and I asked him to write down the name of that treatment. And HE LITERALLY SAID NO. I asked again, and he groaned, and said, "Fine--it's called [this]." I ask him to spell it, and again he groans, then spells it really quickly. Ugh. I should also note that he was also wearing a douchey blackberry headset on his ear the whole time (at least have the respect to take the damn thing off when you're looking between your patient's legs!), and was dressed unprofessionally in too-short, sloppy jeans with white ankle athletic socks and sneakers. Anyway, it turned into this whole ordeal, because at some point, I was so frustrated, stressed, and annoyed that I began to shed tears of anger. And I am *not* someone who cries easily. At the end of the appointment, I called him out on everything--not apologizing for the wait, not introducing himself, and being rude, condescending, dismissive, and unhelpful. He stared blankly at me, and essentially told me that he could tell that I was "smart" and that he knew that I wouldn't be satisfied with his answers, so that's why he wouldn't give me any specific information. Umm...what? At this point, I just wanted this to be over with, so I told him that an apology would be nice, and he gave me this quick "Sorry," like a five year old does when he doesn't really mean it. After he left and I put my clothes on, I asked to speak to the office manager. I told her what had happened, and from her reaction, I had the sense that my experience wasn't the first time something like this happened. At my request, she also gave me a tiny tiny (like maybe 20%) discount off my appointment (I was flat out refusing to pay at this point), and said that if I wanted to make a follow-up appointment with my regular doctor, I'd only have to pay that 20% difference. Ugh. In short, Castelli is a horrible, unprofessional "doctor." Avoid at all costs. [P.S. everything turned out fine, and it really wasn't anything--not that you were wondering.] Tip: Try Dr. Philip Hirshman--he's the antithesis of Castelli and was helpful, considerate, friendly, and a great doctor.

text: I have spent a lot of time all around Mexico. This is the real deal -- it's like eating in a hole in the wall taqueria in Guadalajara. This place is for people who like authentic Mexican low brow food, rather than Tex-Mex or "Gringo" versions of the cuisine. It is also for people who, when they walk in and realize that they are the only non-Mexicans in the joint, view this as a positive sign that "this must be the place" rather than one which engenders self consciousness. I can almost guarantee you will be the only native English speaker in the place (unless I'm there...) As for ambience - there isn't any, which is to say that it's perfect. It's flourescent lights, formica tables and steel chairs with red vinyl. Mexican tv blaring cheesy soap operas or soccer above the counter. Phone cards to call back to Mexico for sale. Just like Guadalara. Now let's talk food. If they don't bring them to you, ask them for some grilled jalapenos. They are fantastic, but be careful. The chips are prepared fresh and the hot sauces in the squeeze containers on the table are home made. The tacos are all-world. "Al Pastor" (spiced pork), "Carne Asada" (grilled steak) and "Camaron" (shrimp) are the best, and come piled high with the filling, cilantro, onion and a lime wedge. At a buck fifty each, they cannot be beat. The tortas are Mexican hot sandwiches. Order the "Carne Desebrada" - pulled beef. It is a meal in itself, with avocado, jalapeno and the most addictively flavored beef you will ever eat. I have friends that swear they are made of heroin. Other standouts include Shrimp Diablo (spicy shrimp), Chile Verde (pork in heavily spiced tomatillo sauce), Burrito al pastor (a burrito with the same filling as the tacos mentioned above), and fajita mixta (fajita with the kitchen sink). There are also lots of other "deeper" Mexican dishes like shrimp cocktail in tomato juice, menudo, various "caldos" and mojarro (a whole fried fish that you pick apart with your fingers). Drinks are Mexican beer, sodas, water, horchata or, if they have it that day, "agua de melon", which is cantaloupe juice that is out of this world. The place is CASH ONLY. Manuel and Ana, the owners, speak decent English. No one else does at all. They will always be there. Finally, back to the ambience/clientelle . I am not going to get into a whole social commentary thing, but if you are the type of person who will get jumpy walking into a dive where the people eating are guys who work landscaping, construction, etc. this is not for you, as this is precisely that place. (I literally hired a guy to do some drywall work for me while having lunch there one day.) But to put your mind at ease, I routinely bring my kids, wife, friends there and we are welcomed like family. No one is going to bite you. You, however, are going to want to bite their food.
