text: I love Santa Barbara and realize they don't want to have the big chain hotels taking over because the city will lose its charm. HOWEVER, I don't see where the boutique hotels get off charging full service Marriott/Hyatt rates. We ended up staying here at Sandman because it was the most reasonably priced, so it seemed. I pulled up in front of the hotel, walked inside the lobby and was greeted by the police officer who was dusting for prints. I was very reluctant to check in since the young lady working the front desk didn't offer any explanation at first. The officer assured me that nothing ever happens there and it would be ok. I checked in and stayed one night. The room was below average. Everyone obviously has different standards of cleanliness (although they shouldn't!). The furniture, carpet, linens were very worn looking and stained. The room had some newer amenities (LCD screen tv, DVD player, and an extremely comfortable mattress. The fridge and microwave were dated. The walls in this place are paper thin and pretty beat up. The bathroom sucked! Low water pressure, and very outdated! It was a cold night so I was pleased that the antiquated wall heater did crank out some good heat. Customer service at this hotel simply doesn't exist. I called the front desk to request a late check out at 1 pm (only 1 hour past regular check out time). I was told to vacate the room immediately as it was already 12 pm. I have stayed at MANY hotels in my life and have NEVER before been denied a late check out. I was waiting for my ride to show up and had several bags. I asked them if they had a cart or something to help me bring my bags to the lobby as I would have to wait for my ride there. She told me that they did not have a cart, it was not a full service hotel. Since when does having a cart make a hotel full service? When I finally got my luggage to the lobby, there was already an unhappy guest screaming at the front desk staff. Once she left, the staff was in the back office with the door wide open bad-mouthing her. I won't be staying here again! Not worth the price even though it's one of the less expensive hotels.
label: NEG

text: Living in a largely Asian populated area you would think that there would be better Chinese food near me, but I guess I was wrong. The entire neighborhood is full of Asian Restaurants serving Americanized food so when they all failed we started ordering once in a while from J.C.'s on 8th street. I was never much of a fan of them growing up, but my husband convinced me to give it a try again...after all if had to be better than what's on 7th street. text: I was this close to giving Pumpkin 5 stars because I've rarely experienced food that's tasted so exquisite. I was here on a Thursday night with a group of 7 for our BYO-of-the-month club's April outing. We started with the octopus and the gnocchi as appetizers for the table - which were both heavenly, but the veggies that came tossed with the gnocchi were so, well, vibrant, if 'vibrant' can be a taste. I do not like cooked carrots, but the carrots in this dish tasted unlike any carrot I had previously had, as did all of the other veggies. What was most intriguing was the way all the components of the dish were so distinct, but perfectly enhanced each other at the same time. Looking for the same revelation with my entree, I ordered the chicken. I was not disappointed. This chicken was succulent, and I've never been able to use that word to describe chicken before. I also had a taste of my friend's scallops, which were delicate, yet meaty and perfectly cooked. Despite being a small BYO, Pumpkin accommodated our large group and a few others that evening quite easily, without making the dining room seem overly crowded. Pumpkin is a smidge on the pricey side and I found the desserts to be so-so, which prevented me from ramping this up to a 5 star review, but any place that can make me wax lyrical over a carrot has got to be tried.

text: My hubby and I took a weekend trip to Nola to check out the French Quarter and attend a concert. Then I found the HGI at the Convention Center (with a little help from Priceline). Our room was clean, the price was decent, the staff was extremely friendly and helpful, the water pressure was great, and all the lights worked. We also really enjoyed checking out some of the Warehouse District haunts on our way to the French Quarter. A few things to note: The beds are small. We got a double, and the second night we ended up sleeping in separate beds b/c we couldn't fit comfortably on one bed together. We're not huge people either. If you have or are planning to find a significant other during your stay, I would recommend getting a king. This hotel is on SOUTH Paul Street, not SAINT Paul Street. I'm sure most of you are smart enough to figure that out, but if you punch "St Paul" into the GPS, it will take you to the wrong place. FYI. Yes, valet parking is $30 a day. Our valet in no way forced us to use this service, but we did anyway for the convenience. If you don't like it, you are welcome to drive around for an hour trying to find a space to park on the street for free until 8AM the next morning when you get ticketed because you're too hungover to remember to move your car. It's your call. Ask the concierge for the name of a licensed cab service (most cabs in Nola aren't). Ok, the hotel wasn't spotless - the hallway carpet was stained, and the walls had marks on them and stuff. However, our sheets were clean (they even smelled clean, which is a first for hotels that I've stayed in), and the bathroom was clean. That was enough to make me happy. Yeah, this hotel isn't dirt cheap, but it's in a great location, it's clean, and the staff is friendly. If you want to stay in a five star hotel, you're going to pay a five star price.

text: Sixteen years ago I adopted the best dog in the whole world. Found in cage number 11, he barked and smiled and barked some more and it was love at first sight. But, the SPCA did not want to let me adopt him. I was young, I rented an apartment, I did not have a property deed. It is understandable to want to ensure that a pet will have a good home. And perhaps promises of undying love and devotion are not enough to warrant the transfer of a dog from a shelter to a stranger. But they made me jump through many hoops: copies of my lease; wanting to talk to my landlord (before cell phones made this possible at the times they were open.) And, they were not very nice. Rude, dismissive, too busy to be bothered, annoyed. Three times I visited hoping to adopt him. And next to me were homeowners (this seemed to be the key) looking at a dog. They clearly stated, "If he doesn't work out we can just bring him back." It was unbelievable that these people, elderly but possessing a property deed, were able to be so brazen about their lack of commitment and still allowed to adopt the dog. Well, the short side of the story is that I did what all young girls are tempted to do when they feel mistreated. I called my father. I am not sure what he did, or who he talked to, but on the fourth day and fourth attempt to adopt Kota, I was granted the privilege of taking him home. We have been together ever since. And I am very thankful to my father for his mysterious assistance. Just recently, 16 years later, I found a dog running lose, trailing his leash behind him in Media. Of course, I grabbed him before he ran into traffic on State Street and proceeded to ask everyone I saw if they knew the dog. Then Sam and I spent several hours going from place to place, pet store, emergency vet, etc. to see if anyone knew where he lived, if he had a micro chip, etc. The Del. Co. SPCA was our last choice. Funny, that ideally it should have been our first choice. But the sentiment was consistent at each place we visited. Perhaps better to keep the dog for a few days and post signs than to drop him off there... In the end we had no choice. We walked into the SPCA and were completely ignored as the staff talked amongst themselves commenting on a recent client...negatively in front of other clients. They seemed disorganized and annoyed (still!) And there Sam and I stood wtih a little dog in our arms...waiting...waiting. Finally we had to be rude to get someone's attention. (What did they think we wanted standing there with this dog anyway?) There is a happy ending. Someone realized she had taken a "Lost Dog" call for the dog we had found. The owners were called and we volunteered to drive the dog home. He never had to be checked into or checked out of the SPCA. It would have been hard to leave him there. If people love animals and want to work with them, I would hope that they would like people who also loved animals and are trying to help them. But it seemed there is no protocol to dealing with people, or communicating, or being helpful. A place to adopt animals should be much friendlier, perhaps cleaner, perhaps more organized.

They even set up big TVs to play the games and let customers rearrange the tables/chairs for better viewing pleasure. Also, the food we did have was pretty stellar and they had a great drink selection! On another visit, my friends and I actually sat down for dinner. Our waiter was very attentive, maybe too much so. Although he was a little awkward, we definitely got everything we could have wanted. Everyone was totally happy with their meal. I've had pizza and sandwiches there, and both were great. I don't regularly venture too close to the University, but when I do, I like to know there are places like Gentle Ben's tucked nearby!
label: POS

text: I was very impressed with Holland House. We walked in with a group of 4 early on a Friday night, without reservations- our mistake! However, we were pleasantly offered a place at the bar, and I must say- I really enjoyed this as a first taste of the wonderful drinks Holland House offers. Our bartender was very attentive. After explaining the history behind the Holland House name, and gin's history and origins- he proceeded to make us several special cocktails not listed on the menu. Everything was painstakingly created and crafted with significant attention to detail. From ice to garnishes to serving glass, I was delighted in their thoughtfulness. Previously not even a fan of gin based cocktails, I was especially impressed with the variety of subtle flavors these drinks showcased. We stayed on for dinner- and the food was really where their superiority to the other glamorous speak-easy style house in Nashville (Patterson House) was clear. Every one of our meals was its own kind of wonderful. I had the pulled pork, my husband had the burger, my sister had the fried chicken, and a friend had the steak special. We shared tastes all around, because each dish was perfectly complemented with unique sides- wonderful creations in their own right. Our ONLY disappointment was dessert- a flat, tasteless whoopie pie. That didn't spoil our fun or our experience- we just had another drink! I have returned, and will do so again. Definitely a diamond in the rough!
label: POS

text: Stay away from Extended Stay. The only thing I wanted to extend was my foot out the door at 2 am because I left early rather than spend 3 more hours here. The elevator is on it's last legs as is the AC. The lamp in my room had some dried funk on the switch from someones greasy hands. I felt like getting a penicillin shot when I was done with this place. Priceline is great, but I felt betrayed when I got to this place. Next time I'm going to the Courtyard Marriot next door.

text: Picture the scenario: You've just flown in from England, you're tired, it's humid, it feels like 1 am and you're hungry. You want food that you know, but you're happy to try some American stuff, too. You want it to be tasty but not too expensive. Sound reasonable? Alright, not if you live in Philly, but you know what I mean... Go to Pub and Kitchen. There's a pub. English style, with pints and everything. And a kitchen. With great food cooked extremely well. I had a dark n stormy (rum and ginger) and it was just what I wanted to wake me up and see me through the night. Then I had the gnocchi, which was quite simply the best I've ever had. Light, crispy on the outside, soft on the inside, wonderfully seasoned with subtle flavors, it was awesome. The salad we shared was simple but great - well dressed and fresh. The burger and salmon also looked very tasty. It's a good spot and it gets the mixture of drinking hole and restaurant absolutely right. The chef is fantastic and the atmosphere is perfect. Far from a sports bar, it does show the game on the screens so you can keep score without it being intrusive on your night out with buddies.

text: Just got back from dinner with my mom and my sisters and after a shaky start, Novita pulled off a win. If only they could teach the Villanova Wildcats how to do that. So I live about 4 doors away and after putting off a visit for a bit of time, I finally made a reservation after finding out my 3 moms were coming to town for the flower show. After walking around the flower show and hanging at my crib for an hour they were famished. We walked over for our 8 o'clock reservation, which I confirmed with the owner to find out that they took the reservation, they just didn't hold they reservation. Which is really, the most important part. Needless to say, I'm pissed at this point. If I didn't live a 10 second walk away, we would've bailed. We sucked it up and killed some time and salsa at my place until 8:30. When we walked back in, I told the host/waiter that we were returning for a missed reservation. He took the cue to start busting my balls and said that they have no tables. Me being the hothead that I am, came thisclose to losing it but he started laughing and took us to our table. Once seated with a glass of wine in front of me, I was completely disarmed. From there it was a treat of North African and Mediterranean flavors. The mussel appetizer on special in a Morrocan sauce had great flavor as did the regular mussels in white wine. My braised lamb shank over couscous was so tender, that my fork cut right through it. My sister's lamb merguez had an awesome cuminy bite to them, while sis #2 had a delicious porcini ravioli. My mom's clean plate confirmed that her picky palate even approve of the breaded chicken entree. Being the sweettooth's that we are we eagerly ordered dessert. My pecan tart came with a vanilla gelato that was so close to ice cream, that I was completely fooled. My sister raved about the lightness of her creme brûlée and my mom and other sister lamented that they could've eaten 3 orders of their chocolate mousse. All on all, novita had a skilled hand with their house made desserts (rare for such a small space). I wish I would've checked in on my neighbor sooner for dinner, but I look forward to being drawn back even after I move out this spring.
label: POS

text: Ok, the yogurt here isn't really that great and the consistency is poor (the term watery comes to mind...it shouldn't melt before you've paid for it.) But it's the service that really gets me down. I was in the Goleta location before Valentine's Day and while I was at the register, I saw a big ad for a free yogurt with gift card purchase of $25 or more. So I asked if I could get a gift card (perfect Valentine pick me up for a dateless friend, no?) The person at the register could not speak English. Which meant she could not understand me at all. I picked up the sign, turned it around and showed it to her. She was still clueless. She shrugged and said, "Sorry" her one word in English and made no attempt to help me further. In fact, she tried to just ring me up for the yogurt I had and be done with it. It was only when I insisted she get someone else to help me that she irritatedly went into the back to get someone else. It's worth mentioning at this point that the place was empty. I doubt I would have held up a line, but I was starting to get a bit principle happy. A man came out who spoke English. But, shockingly, it didn't help that much! He couldn't understand why I wanted the free yogurt with my gift card, even though it was clearly stated as the HOOK for the ad. He thought, I guess that I'd give the free yogurt to the person with the gift card? I'm not sure. I finally convinced him that giving me the free yogurt was the best deal for HIM since my yogurt was 9 oz when the ad said up to 16 oz. He agreed and I got my free yogurt and was ALLOWED to pay for my gift card. Honestly, people. If someone can't speak enough English to serve a customer, how exactly can they apply the rules of food safety or read a label properly? I'm not saying everyone has to be fluent. Clearly, we are a free society and everyone has to start someplace. But one has to question the management of this place when they can't manage to have someone who can communicate or CARE when someone wants to spend about five times the average purchase. Frankly, even if they got it together customer service wise, I'd probably not return due to the low quality of the product.

text: It's my own fault for trying several times to make this a viable alternative to the Post Office or anywhere else that could satisfy assorted mailing / packaging / notary needs. Don't make the same mistake. Go to a notary or the post office. This last two occurrences pushed me over the edge. On the 12th of April I mailed 4 IRS packages. I mailed them UPS 2 day. 4 days later only 3/4 had arrived. I had continuously checked on-line for their status but couldn't report them until it had passed it's expected delivery date by one day. I chatted with the customer service person at MBE and was assured it was in transit and I should follow up with UPS. Low and behold, a call to UPS revealed that the missing package had NEVER been received. The package NEVER left MBE until I called them and PROVED, through UPS, that it had never been sent. Second issue... I mailed out 38 invites. Each was a square envelope and I needed them hand stamped so that the invites inside weren't damaged or wrinkled. The postage required was $0.69. I was charged $1.18 EACH. I wasn't told the postage was $0.69, only that it would be $1.18 for each. I assumed with the shape (square envelopes are always extra) that was a decent charge. After paying, I asked to see one of the envelopes so I had an idea of what they would look like with the hand stamped postage mark. When it was handed to me to look at I saw the $0.69 postage mark. I asked why the charge was so expensive and why it wasn't disclosed - and the clerks EXACT WORDS we're "If I wasted my time explaining charges to everyone all day i'd never get anything done." So instead they charged double the postage and treated me to free attitude. I will never use MBE again. This location or any other. Not worth the risk to whatever i'm sending.

text: It's your final day in Philly before you fly back to London and it's the middle of summer and steaming. You need to cool down but you want to make the most of your time. What do you do? You could do a lot worse than to visit the Franklin Institute. There are so many interesting and varied exhibits, with plenty for the whole family. There are shows of different types, including IMAX and simulators. There are fun competitions and do-it-yourself experiments as well as a great shop with puzzles, games and memorabilia. You could spend the whole day here or just walk around half of it and come back at a later date. There are all sorts of packages of shows and exhibits available, making it fun and educational for everyone. P.S. One thing. If you go to the shark show expecting blood and guts, you'll be disappointed. But you might just fall in love with a whale shark. P.P.S. There's nothing at all wrong with falling in love with a whale shark.

text: From the second we walked into the park I was pleasantly surprised. It looks beautiful and inviting from the entrance gate. The first thing we did was head to the gift shop. It was huge. They had such a great selection, including infant products, which was perfect because I have a 7 month old who needed a hat. (about $6). I also picked up a stuffed white alligator in the Louisiana Swamp section, and it was only $3.99. The prices were great. Usually you go to a theme park gift shop, and the prices are outrageous that you can only afford to pick up one thing. Prices on the refreshments, that's another story. I paid almost $3 for a fountain drink, and $12 at the Haagen Dazs for a shake and cup of ice cream! Geeze. Talk about raping my wallet. I'd recommend taking your own beverages, and food because they don't check your bags and there is a large lawn area to have picnics on. We arrived at the Zoo at 11:00 AM and didn't leave until 3:30 PM. There was so much to do!!! You also felt like you could reach the animals they were so close. That was so great. Actually, we went to see the Giraffes, and I was only about 10 inches away from reaching the Giraffe when it tilted it's head over the railing towards us. The reptile section was amazing. It was an entire building dedicated towards all different types of reptiles. My husband really loved it. There were so many different types of snakes, I lost count! The Louisiana Swamp area was my favorite, and probably one of the largest exhibits. They had a huge swamp with green water, and filled with about 10 Alligators! There is a deck built above it all so you can just look down an observe all of it. They also had a Raccoon and Nutria exhibit. It was a lot of fun!!! It was such a great experience for my little girl. She really loved it all! It was entertaining for all of us, and I can't wait to go back! The only complaint I have is the parking situation. We got there early, only about an hour after the park was open and there was no where to park. They don't have a section that you pay for parking, or that is just excluded to the people who are visiting the zoo, so anyone who is visiting the area can park there. We actually had to park in one of the local soccer fields adjacent to the parking lot, but it wasn't a far walk so it wasn't too bad. So get there early if you can!

text: While the Vet held some good memories for me, Citizen's Bank Park is a thousandfold improvement over the Vet. There really are no bad seats in the entire park, and the food is great. In fact, the Food Network gave CB Park an award for the best baseball stadium food in the U.S. during it's award ceremonies this year. The park is also a great place to watch Ryan Howard hit home runs (I love when they ring the bell) and to watch the Phillies try not to blow it against whatever team they happen to be playing (you can get a fancy new park, but the Phillies are still sure to let me down season after season... yet I keep coming back). I was especially happy about CB Park's dollar dog nights, but I got sick the last time that I had dollar hot dogs there. It's probably just my touchy digestive system, which gets nauseated easily, so my advice is to find out which nights they offer dollar dogs and eat as many as you can handle. It's a good deal, especially since stadium food is usually overpriced. Another highlight is the Chickie & Pete's stand b/c they sell crab fries (with or without cheese). That's pretty much all they sell, aside from something to drink. It's $5.50 for fries w/o cheese, $7.00 if you want cheese. Just get in line before the game starts b/c you'll be in line a while. Chickie and Pete's stand is very popular. In all, I really like Citizen's Bank Park. I just wish that sports stadiums weren't named after corporations or banks b/c 1) they suck as far as names go and 2) the name has to change every time the corporation gets taken over by another one. Remember how the Corestates Center became the FU Center, which became the Wachovia Center? I miss the good old days when our stadiums were named after people, like JFK Stadium. Oh well.

text: I'm giving this place one star because zero stars isn't an option. I adore food... I love everything about it. As far as the food, our raw oysters were unfresh and slightly cooler than room-temperature. I found my boyfriend, an oyster purist who prefers the flavors of the gulf to gratuitous cocktail saucery and lemon juice, loading up his fodder with the available ketchup-and-horseradish mixture just to give it any flavor at all. The "chargrilled" oysters were just sad. Maybe I've been spoiled by Drago's and Acme, but presenting a plate of tired oysters covered in what tasted like shaker-can Parmesan cheese and residual grease is just wrong! I'm not trying to be a bitch, but putting out quality food isn't That difficult, and for $68.00, I expected better. Don't be fooled by the enticing window display and come-hither seafood boil smell - save yourself the frustration and expense and go somewhere else.

text: The Venture Inn has been a tradition in the somewhat seedy world of the Gay-borhood of Philadelphia. With more and open acceptance of different life styles, however, new, upscale, expensive and even outstanding eateries have popped up all over the place in the Washington Square area that cater to mainly a gay clientele, and therefore some of the old places have been left behind. The Venture is one of them. Although a "grand dame" of the community, it nonetheless has been left behind and nowadays caters to mainly an adult community, from which the moniker "The Denture Inn" has emerged. Although unjust, its reputation continues despite new management and what seems to be an honest effort at changing its character. The small side street where Venture is Camac Street, one of the numerous alley-type streets all over the older part of Philadelphia. These small streets have become more pricey and upscale, however, Camac has maintained a sort of seedy reputation due to its commercial employment. We went to the Venture Inn just to see how things had changed. I'm afraid they haven't sufficiently to go there again. In four categories, service, food, ambiance, and price, it loses to the neighboring establishments. First the service. Our waiter was obviously used to the older crowd and seemed to want to be our friend from the start. Frankly, if I wanted to be friends with a waiter, I'd make it outside of a restaurant. His overtures seemed pedantic, especially compared to the mediocre service we got which included forgetting a round of drinks we ordered with dinner. Second, the food. The mussels I ordered came in a tasty sauce. However, there were several unopened, bad ones. That is something any good restaurant would be able to screen. The food was generally good, although the presentation was "homey", not what you would expect for the price. No espresso. Third, the ambiance. On a beautiful cool summer evening in Philadelphia, al fresco seating would have been a plus. The Venture Inn restaurant sits in a building where the smoke stench has permeated the walls over decades and decades. The yellowish walls attest to the nicotine and tar of the pre-smoke prohibition in Philadelphia. Frankly, I was gasping for breath after an hour. Fourth, the price. We spent forty per person including a glass of wine each. Right around the corner, I can get the same at an upscale, new, saucy Mixto restaurant that features Cuban/Colombian infusion with knock-your-socks off service and outstanding ambiance and food. It is obvious by the clientele surrounding us that the Venture is happily within its core clientele of tired gay men in their 60s to whom a disrespectful out-of-shape waiter and mediocre food is a compliment.
label: NEG

text: Tropicana Field is the worst stadium in professional sports. It's no more or less attractive than the old Metrodome, but it lacks all of that ballpark's atmosphere and charm. First, it's in a sea of asphalt parking lots and interstate onramps. Second, the stadium was barely two-thirds full for a Saturday afternoon game against the Yankees. Third, the fans who had showed up to support the Rays appeared confused by the rules and etiquette of baseball. Lots of cowbell slamming at inopportune times. This increased late in the game, despite the fact that the team was being no-hit into the 8th. As seemed to be a rule in the Tampa area generally, many fans were powerfully intoxicated, and the hour of day seemed to be no deterrent. Fans started leaving in the 7th inning. If I can sit in pouring rain in the Bronx to watch Daniel Cabrera almost no-hit my team, Tampans should be able to sit in this air conditioned pod for the same chance at history. Concessions were expensive, nearly matching YS prices, and disgusting. Are there seriously Outback Steakhouse concession stands all over this ballpark? Apparently, because people who couldn't bother to sit down or wait until inning breaks to inconvenience their neighbors kept milling through rows with bloomin' onions and some sort of nauseating chipped beef flatbread. Finally, one likes to walk around a new stadium to see it from different angles. Our walk around the field level concourse felt like a teaser for the special that premiered on the National Geographic Channel this past weekend: Solitary Confinement. No field views, and a long walk through concrete tunnels. And the line for the Rays touch tank was probably two innings long. Seriously? This team should move to Sioux City immediately. They'd get much better fan support. And a nicer ballpark.

text: I went to Bacco with a group of 5 people total on a Friday evening around 8 p.m. We'd just arrived in town for Mardi Gras and wanted to kick off the weekend with some delicious food in a classy restaurant. When we arrived at Bacco reservation-less, we expected to wait but were seated in only a few minutes, which was a pleasant surprise. The restaurant itself is quite large for a French Quarter place, so I think they have enough space to accommodate any dinner-time rushes. We were given water and menus and the waiter started to reel off the nightly specials... ...when suddenly a GIANT COCKROACH sprinted across the floor, ran up and over the waiter's shoe, did a little dance under our table (causing myself and the other girl to give embarrassing little screeches of shock and instantly lift our feet up off the floor), then proceeded to zip around the immediate area while the waiter stood there open-mouthed. He choked out a fragmented apology, said he'd never seen that before, and excused himself, presumably so he could go talk to his manager to see what he should do. While he was off getting marching orders, one of the men of our group decided that he'd better do something about the situation, because the cockroach had taken up residence under our table and us girls were severely disgusted. He bravely slew the vermin and left its broken body near the head of the table; we didn't know what to do with it. When the waiter returned, he offered to take us to another table, but we demurred; after all, the damn thing was dead! The cockroach's body stayed where it was for the remainder of our meal. For the cockroach, I'll remove one star; it's not something I'd expect to ever see in a classy restauarnt, but hey, it's the French Quarter during Mardi Gras, I'll cut them some slack. But the other two stars were lost as a result of purely shoddy service. After ordering our salads, I decided to order a glass of wine while ordering my entree. Our salads came... our entree came... and finally, after I was more than halfway done with my Lobster and Shrimp Ravioli (which was delicious!), my wine finally came. This was after several reminders to our waiter. Our water cups frequently stood empty, which is not a forgivable offense especially when we had to ask for more water several times. We were offered a refill on bread about midway through our meal, which we eagerly said yes to; this bread never materialized and we sadly gave up on it when the waiter brought us our check. However, I do like to be left mostly alone while I eat, and this wait staff was great about not bothering us... however I think that was more due to their incompetence and less due to any attempt to help their guests better enjoy their meal. After our meal, our waiter asked if we wanted dessert, and we all replied that we were full. He then said that because of the cockroach incident, he had been authorized to offer us one dessert for free. Are you kidding me?! We just told you we weren't hungry, first of all, so you should probably think of something else; second of all, what kind of manager do have, that he's authorized you to give ONE dessert for FIVE people?! But that was the meager offering to make us feel a little better about the gooey crushed body that was STILL lying next to our waiter's foot. At the end of the night, we requested separate checks, and at our waiter's request, let him know once again what we'd each had; yet he still managed to charge the wrong meals to the wrong credit cards, which meant we had to wait 10 minutes while he corrected that error. I suppose I should say something about the food: It was good. It was what I expected to get, for the price. The flavors were excellent and unique but it didn't make me want to sing it from the rooftops. Personally, I won't be returning to Bacco; it just wasn't good enough to warrant that.
label: NEG

In retrospect, I should never have ordered a saran-wrapped pastry from a huge pile in a shop that can't possibly move more than a handful of them on a regular day. I'm sure SEPTA is doing what it can with the finding it gets, and I think it's terrible that Pennsylvania doesn't recognize that an efficient public transportation system is extremely important to everyone, not just those with low incomes. But honestly, using SEPTA is a nightmare. If you rely on the bus system to get to work, God bless you. Some bus routes run regularly enough, but most are consistently running late--if they show up at all. I have had in service busses blow right past me on more than one occasion. I have waited for upwards of an hour for a bus. The subway system is utterly useless. We need more lines. Why isn't there a subway line running up and down Columbus? Why isn't there a line that goes up Passyunk? Why isn't there anything but the Orange Line servicing North Philadelphia? And what the hell are we doing with all of these trolley tracks? The regional rail is wasting money. If we modeled it after PATCO and eliminated the conductors we could save a lot of money. Sure the elimination of jobs will be devastating to some, but I think in this case it is for the greater good.

text: Well, you get what you pay for. Yes, the St. Louis Art Museum (SLAM) is free. Not free as in "well technically it's free but we still pressure you into a donation", or free as in "the museum is free but you pay $20 to park", it's completely free. The only thing that costs money are the special exhibitions, food, and the gift shop. You can literally walk right through the doors and head straight to whatever gallery you want. I'm a huge art lover. When I go on trips I always make art museums top of my list of places to visit. I've been to museums large and small, in huge cities and small towns, so I have some experience in this. And the conclusion for my hometown museum? Meh, it's alright. For those uninitiated, SLAM is undergoing a large expansion that will increase their space for 20th and 21st century art. Unfortunately, this is long overdue. They've been stuck in the same building for over 100 years and due to a stipulation in the city's charter, cannot charge admission to the museum. They get their primary revenue through donations and a special tax district that covers most of the St. Louis area. Ok, so the good news is that they're in the process of expanding, which should put them back in the running of being about the size they need to be to be relevant in the art world. But 2 pieces of bad news: #1: The expansion is being delayed due to stricter lending procedures (the museum claims the all the funding is in place however, which I am slightly skeptical of in this economy). #2: Until the expansion takes place, large parts of the museum are closed off or empty, citing vibrations caused by construction. So essentially we are left with 2/3rds of a museum that wasn't all that big to begin with. This is really unfortunate, considering construction will take place for several years, and with everything beling delayed, there is not much light at the end of the tunnel. People visiting the museum for the next 2-3 years will have to live with looking at a lot of empty galleries and missing out on a lot of great art that would normally be displayed. That being said, what is left is good for a few hours of visiting. The Impressionist collection is small but well-represented with important pieces from all the masters. In fact, the same can be said for many of the collections, including the Asian Art, Design, Renaissance Art, and Egyptian Art collections. However, SLAM is probably most well-known in the art world as having some of the preeminent art of German Expressionists, made in the years following WWII. Several galleries exhibit this, culminating with an entire hall of Max Beckmann paintings. I myself am a huge contemporary art fan, but it seems that SLAM is underrepresented in this category. Yes, there's a Lichtenstein and a Warhol or two, and a few Stellas, but when it comes to art created in say...the last 30 years, there are not nearly enough pieces that exhibit the breadth of the titanic shifts in the art world during this time. In other cities, the local Contemporary Art museum picks up the slack for these voids, but without a permanent collection, the St. Louis Contemporary has only rotating exhibitions. Presumably, the expansion will solve this problem, as well as other problems, such as having only a small cafe to eat at (and not a very good one at that). But until then, people will have to make due with only 2/3rds of a museum. Without the galleries closed off, I can only give the museum 3 stars, but in its current state I can't justify more than 2 stars. Rest assured I'll update my review when the expansion is complete, and I hope to be able to up it to 4 or 5 stars, but in the meantime, you get what you pay for, and remember that admission is always free.

Even beyond the embarrassingly drunk douchebags gyrating all over the place and the music so loud you couldn't even hear the company, it literally took me AN HOUR to get ONE DRINK, and that was sitting right at the bar, hemmed in on all sides by a surging crowd. text: There are a number of reasons to love Philly, but Ortleib's is reason enough to make we want to go back and take some friends. I was in town for a week (business trip) in July 2007; my first visit to Philly. I followed the Yelp reviews to the Sunday jam session on a solo expedition. I caught a cab from my downtown hotel and, yes, the neighborhood does look a little shady. But as soon as I opened the cab door, the sound from inside beckoned me and, boy, am I glad I went. I walked in at around 9pm and the place was hopping. Three instrumentalists were jamming on stage, while a fourth 20-something lady was tap dancing. I took a seat at the bar, sipped a couple glasses of wine, chatted with the owner and a waitress, and just soaked in the great local vibe. There seemed to be a good mix of ages and races in attendance, and everyone was smiling and having a blast. Sunday was so much fun that I went back on Tuesday, this time with three co-workers in tow. (more than 4 people should probably call ahead) Even with a good crowd, we were able to secure a table shortly after arriving. We enjoyed several rounds of beer & wine and spicy sweet potato fries, and just totally dug the music. There was an especially great pianist that night. After a couple hours, we decided to check out another spot in the neighborhood, at the nearby Standard Tap. Our short walk from Ortlieb's after midnight was completely uneventful. Although I encourage everyone to always be cautious in unfamiliar neighborhoods at night, the streets were pretty quiet and not the least bit menacing.

text: The River Room played host to my first event booking at this location. I programmed a make-up show to fulfill my contractual obligations to the artist Chris Pureka, whom I'd booked at the now defunct Siena Spa Hotel & Casino. Owner Chuck Shapiro and his staff were very accommodating to my ideas to make the locale concert ready for the critically acclaimed New England based Pureka, who'd been the recent recipient of rave reviews from Billboard magazine and The NY Times for her new album How I learned to See in the Dark. I brought in lighting by Rick Patton and staging by Mac's Stage Rentals with a sound system provided by Duke Goff. The undercard (Athena McIntyre, Mel Wade and Lacey Mattison) performed superb opener sets in support of the headliner Pureka. What was impressive was the vibe in the room and the excellent service by servers Kayla, Shaunessy, bartender Meagan and the manager Rich. Chris Pureka did an amazing 70-minute set that thrilled and captivated the assembled 75+ guests. The sound reinforcement Shapiro had installed weeks back to control ambient conversational chatter, really helped the room's sonic warmth. The audience could hear every lyric from the high-mountain Americana the artist shared with her rapt attendees. Food came out fast, even though the place was jam packed beyond capacity. The plating of the dozen or so dishes I watched people enjoy was artful and immaculate. I ordered the spicy prawns over long penne pasta, and it just might have been the best dish I've had in Reno. The mushrooms, marinated red peppers and prawns were succulent and absolutely delicious. The aroma of the dish brought a gaggle of friends over to my area to investigate my delight. The portion was just right, as I hate to be hungry after an entree. If you're looking for comfortable and posh, with a scenic view of the lovely Truckee River in winter, an exceptional dining experience awaits at The River Room.

text: Really more of a 3.5 stars but I am willing to give it 4 for now. The wine bar element has not been set up yet, so I will update once they have their full selection up and running. Turned out to be The Black Keys. Service: We came at the end of the night so they were winding down but they were friendly and accommodating to my many questions. Not sure how they hold up during peak hours but they seem pretty enthusiastic about their opening, I hope they keep it up! Food: For starters, we tried their beets and the roasted romanesco. The beets were ok. I wanted the goat cheese to have a bit more tang to cut through the sweetness of the beets. Also, I could have done without the parsley which was a bit overpowering. The roasted romanesco was nice but I wish it had come warm. Also their raisins are marinated in quite the vinaigrette. It'll give your mouth a bit of a pinch/punch ... Now to the stars of the show... that pizza crust! Mmm Mmmm Mmmm! I'd like to sleep on a bed made of their pizza dough/crust... a good night's sleep with a good night's eat! It was a little crisp with some nice charr on the edges but still fluffy and a bit chewy. If you don't like these characteristics on your crust... well then... more for me & my bed ... We had the Kennett and the Margherita. I really enjoyed the Kennett (bechamel, mushrooms, rosemary AND onions) and the bf would have too but was a bit put off by the surprise onions that came on top. The menu didn't say it had onions but it does. So just beware for any fellow onion haters out there. The Margherita was standard, we really just ordered to eat more crust... Drinks: Til they get their liquor license they are offering complimentary selections of wine & beer. However, I will return once their wine bar is up and running. I am happy to see a pizza & wine bar combo swing into the area but their starters were a bit off and as much as their aesthetic is nice, having the menus on chalkboard was hard on the eyes, esp with the dim lighting. They have very reasonable prices and I am looking forward to sampling their red wine selection. Now about making me that bed of pizza ....

text: I'm not an Asian food aficionado by any means. Though I do enjoy Chinese food, before moving to Nashville my main exposure to it was at the buffet line of various establishments typically run by Latinos that included taquitos, fried chicken, and chocolate pudding right next to the sweet and sour chicken. International Market was my first taste of something different. Now, I know that International Market isn't the pinnacle of Asian cuisine. It's not even my favorite Chinese restaurant in town (that honor goes to Chinatown near Green Hills Mall). But International Market was there first, so it gets a nod. The staff at IM are always very quick and courteous, which considering this is a cafeteria style eatery, that puts you in the right state of mind right from the start. The Chinese options are fairly typical fare, but they are all consistent and tasty. I suggest the pepper steak over some fried rice if you're a first timer and not a vegetarian. I'm also addicted to the chicken on a stick, because really, any food on a stick automatically gets points just for being on a stick, right? And for dessert, skip the confections by the checkout counter, and opt instead for the fried sweet potatoes, lightly battered in tempura batter, which they've had all but one time when I've been there and are absolutely delicious. I can't speak for the Thai options that IM has, but my girlfriend has had the Pad Thai with fried tofu on many occasions and has always enjoyed it. International Market may not be the best place in Nashville for Asian food, but for the price (we always eat for far less than twenty bucks) and the portions, you really can't beat it for a good, quick, cheap meal.

text: There is peace in the gentle scrape slide of the pucks along the sanded court. All is well on a Friday night at the shuffleboard courts - the world's largest. The regulars are generally gray and host tournaments throughout the year (weather allowing). Friday nights are different, though. The dollar admission becomes a requested donation, somebody hooks up their iPod to the sound system, and a broad spectrum of the St. Pete demographic turns out to play. Hip kids drink pouch wine and PBR from cups next to families out to explore or enjoy the friendly company. Dates are had - the game is conducive to conversation. Every few weeks, a local cultural organization (think Indian or Polish) hosts a Friday night party. Look for awesome homemade food, exotic music and dance, and the universal sense of acceptance inherent in any event that brings diverse neighborhoods together.

text: I too had the pleasure of meeting Jeremy on the Cloud Climbers Tour. This is the perfect way to spend a weekend get-away in Santa Barbara. I think we did the Buttonwood, Wine World, Kalyra, and Indiana-Jones-Set-Maker Winery place tour. Then at the end, we also took the back roads across the mountains back to the ocean. Everything about the experience was wonderful. The lady friend and I didn't know anything about wine. But everyone was so welcoming that we never felt intimidated. We loved the cabernet and merlot from Buttonwood, but the real treat was Wine World. Wine World is a small wine store tucked away in the town where they buy the sandwiches for lunch from (i think i had prosciutto, goat cheese and pesto in mine). There we had the sweetest chardonnay, several nice muscatos, and a stand out Gewurztraminer. Apparently, the Gewurztraminer was specifically designed to be paired with Thai food. Whether a marketing gimmick or not, we bought it, found some take out Thai food, and loved every second of it. Off roading after going through your first wine tasting trip (where some of us didn't pour out any of our wines) may not be the most comfortable thing in the world. But it sure was exciting, with great views of the ocean and some good old California charm. It really takes you away from the city life we've all become numb to. Plus, the SMALL groups is a huge bonus. It's much more intimate and your chances of being stuck on a tour with a lightweight like me is drastically minimized. All in all, this was the best way to see the Santa Ynez wineries. It was fairly priced, we came home with tons of different wines, and we had fun. Oh also, we got a flat on the freeway right after we finished going over the hills on our way back. Jeremy pulls over and we're next to an orange grove right where the mountains meet the ocean. The clouds were whizzing past us and it was super sunny but nice and cool at the same time. We even saw a pair of California king snakes sliding around in the rocks. (They move a lot faster than I would have ever imagined). Anyways within 20 minutes of Jeremy radioing in HQ, a new jeep was there and we were on our way. Not a single rider had a sour look on their face. You'd figure in most situations like this, you'd get someone who'd start throwing a fit or something. But we were all having SO much fun, that we just soaked up the nice 20 mins of buzzed sunbathing and we were on our merry way.

text: The main problem I have with Sportsman's has been that I visited it with a group of people at 6pm on Wednesdays for years and nearly every time the service was so bad it was laughable (and we have many notes from the evenings about it too). What I learned on the patio over the years before our group left: 1) If at a group, anyone pays and has to leave, you can expect service to stop to the table. Your waiter will look occasionally to see if the rest of you are done. 2) If seated and nobody has come to see you in 10 minutes they forgot you. We ran the clock up to an hour and 15 minutes one time before going in to grab drinks, at an hour and 17 minutes we had a waitress. 3) If it's 6pm / happy hour, you must order every drink you're going to want for the next hour at that point as you're most likely not going to get a second drink order in before happy hour ends at 7. 4) No matter how you try to contact the manager electronically or by leaving messages, you will never get a call back unless you're wanting to rent the place out - we tried seeing if we could get an extension on the drink specials if we were bringing in an average of more than $200 a gathering, and were never able to get a second round of drinks due to nobody ever coming back out to serve us. Calls and emails went unreturned, so did our business. 5) If you have a really good waiter, they will be gone and never back there the next time you're there. 6) If you sit on the patio and there're 3 waiters working, you will be told that the reason service is so slow is that the 1 waiter you've got is also handling the largest table inside. If you happen to go inside there will be one table of 6-8 people and another table or two of 2 people and no particular reason evidenced to why there's no way to get a second round of drinks before happy hour ends. 7) If you have an event that will pay off immediately and not over the course of 4 -6 weeks in profits, you will receive a call in under a day. Learned this when we had contacted them about how much money our group was spending and one of the group also contacted them for a private party for work. That's about that. The food is average, there're a couple of vegetarian options and they're ok but not good bar food. on a 2-4-1 they serve you both beers at once, which means they're warm by #2 unless you're a hardcore alcoholic. I, and the group I'm with, want to love this place (it was home for years in spite of the service) but we've consistently been treated like we're an imposition, and the place is always less than 1/4th capacity when we're there so it's not like we're taking up space, and our bills and tips are high enough. That's my review, mostly seen from the patio as that's the reason we went to Sportsman's. We have not been back in a while. text: I'm a New Orleans transplant -- so I was extremely excited to see a true snowball stand open in Nashville. The snowballs are the real deal, really delicious. Fellow New Orleans folks will appreciate that they have Spearmint under the counter (just ask) and will happily offer you a straw :) If you're new to the snowball scene, though, here's what you need to know: A snowball is not a snowcone. A snowcone is what you get at the circus -- it's course ice with maybe a few flavor choices. It tends to end up as a block of ice that's difficult to eat. A snowball is finely shaved ice that holds the flavors well (and there are a plethora to choose from...) Tanisha is the owner, and most of the time you'll see her or her husband manning the stand. If they don't have a line, it's really a joy to talk to them both. If snowballs aren't your thing, though I'm not sure that's possible -- they have a bunch of other dessert options -- candy, glazed nuts, soft serve, etc. Fleur de Lis is my favorite dessert place in Nashville, and it's been a great excuse to get out to the Farmer's Market more often.

text: I stopped in at The Handcrafted Cookie Company last night on Main Street in Phoenixville (near Brown's Cow!). Here's how it works: You choose your cookie from four cookie types listed on the board as being served that day. You can also choose to bring home cookie dough of any type that they also list on the board. I visited the website (www.thehandcraftedcookiecompany.com) this morning and I see that they want to make available a cookie subscription, which I thought would be really cool, though it appears that the link is not yet live. They also sell something that I look forward to trying called "Bubble Tea". It's a cold beverage that contains tapioca in the bottom of the cup that can be eaten afterwards. Theresa told me that she and Chad lived in Philadelphia near Chinatown for five years and learned about bubble tea from a storeowner there, discovered that they really couldn't get it anywhere else, and wanted to feature it in their own store. Everything they sell is organic, using evaporated cane juice for sugar in their cookies, and they grind their own organic spices as they need them. Your order is baked when you place it. They also told me that they want to make the coffee that they serve available in bean form someday. Chad told me that they use a Colorado coffee company that roasts small batches of beans and delivers them the next day for their retailer's use. They sell Rishi Teas (www.rishi-tea.com) and have an information leaflet at the register about White, Green, Oolong, Black, and Pu-erh Tea which lists the health benefits of each. They sell Fizzy Lizzy beverages (www.fizzylizzy.com) in flavors that come in at least 60% fruit juice and have no added cane sugar, colors, or gums, in flavors such as Lone Star Grapefruit, Costa Rican Pineapple, and Red Hill Pomegranate. The store has two tables with four chairs available for on-site consuming. I thought it would be a great place to bring the kids. I plan on frequenting it often because I feel really good about being able to feed my kids something that they like that also meets my organic standards. Just an aside, the owners also took the time to place a tiny triple trash can in the customer area with trash and recycling separated. text: I kept hearing great things about this spot from a few people @ work and despite never trying the fabled combination of chicken and waffles before, I had no doubt it would meet all my expectations: crispy, juicy, seasoned; moist meat; a crunchy yet chewy waffle; lovely syrupy salty combination. But the fried chicken was completely mediocre. Limp, flavorless skin and pedestrian flavor. For a place that headlines chicken, not frying it correctly puts it below average. We had the tot-choes and a couple of chicken/waffle plates, both white and dark meat. Decor and service is fine, but it looks like they're still struggling with how to execute.

text: This sad excuse for a restaurant is "parroting" every other Newtown casual dining experience. Lackluster food. Earnest but awful service. An okay environment. And the strangest mix of 20-something college kids and 50-something divorcees. It has no sense of identity--at once a sports bar and a quiet pub. The concept lacks discipline and focus, and Newtown still lacks a decent place to grab a casual dinner.

text: honestly I'm astounded by some of the negative reviews here, especially the 1 star review. This is hands down one of my favorite places to eat in Santa Barbara. the food couldn't be fresher, the bloody mary's are to die for and the service is flat out amazing. I can't believe that I have lived in Santa Barbara for five years and only had the pleasure of eating at here just three weeks ago! I had heard amazing things about it and have been wanting to eat here for a while and almost by accident my boyfriend and I wound up hungry and stranded at the harbor. We didn't have to wait long for a perfect table on the balcony, we had clam chowder, fried shrimp, and the hot combination platter. the combo platter was to die for. garlic baked clams, oysters rockefeller, mussels and clams and shrimp dripping in butter and sauce. yum. yum. yum. In the past two weeks we have gone back twice. bringing more and more people with us each time. It is quickly becoming my favorite spots for seafood, you can just taste how fresh everything is. Also the downstairs clam bar is going to be my new hang out. One eyed jack consistently makes the most amazing bloody mary's. The atmosphere is down to earth, friendly, and local. I can't think of Brophy's honestly without smiling like a lunatic. It's been a while since a restaurant in Santa Barbara has excited me this much. just keep in mind this isn't a "fine dining" establishment. This is honest, good, fresh seafood at fair prices. It is always packed, especially during the summer, we went last night (monday) and we waited for 45 minutes. But don't let that deter you, just keep it in mind and give yourself extra time for the wait, and use it as an excuse to meet Jack at the clam bar and taste one of his glorious Bloody Mary's.

text: I have been to Buddakan several times and I'm a bit obsessed, so I was pretty excited when a friend (with a $125 gift card! SCORE!) suggested Pod. Stephen Starr did a fantastic job with the layout. Sadly, we weren't seated in a pod, but we all agreed that we need to come back so we can get the chance to have dinner in one. Since we were going out drinking later, we all decided that sushi would be a bad idea, so we opted to share a few dishes. We ordered martini's and I chose the Blue Martini first, which tasted like tropical fruit. It was ok, not great. Since Pod serves the food as it is done, our Edamame came out first, which was nice, because we could sit and chat and have drinks while still munching on something. The Crab Spring Rolls, Butter Poached Lobster and Grilled Teryaki Salmon were all decent, but I don't think I'd order them again. Especially the lobster. The bok choy and tofu just didn't seem to work well with the lobster. However, the Asian Braised Short Ribs and Wasabi Crusted Filet were TO. DIE. FOR. Absolutely delicious. Loved the Udon noodles with the short ribs and the wasabi mashed potatoes that came with the Filet were delicious. So moral of the food story: stick to the red meat. While we were eating, the manager convinced my friend and I to try the Orange Martini after finishing our first round. It was ok. It was mixed with carrot juice and ginger...but it was a little heavy on the ginger and whatever spices they used. I think it would be a great drink to pair with some sushi, but it was a little tough to drink. To make it up to us, the manager brought over a free round of the Yellow Martini, which ended up being my favorite. I LOVE passionfruit, and the tartness of the drink was great. A friend ordered the green tea gin and tonic, which was seriously refreshing and delicious. We tried the Fluffernutter Spring Rolls and the sorbet, which was a perfect end to the night. We racked up a pretty serious bill by the end of the night, but luckily we had a nice friend to share her gift card with us. Next time, I don't plan on ordering as much, but dammit, I want to sit in a pod! And make sure you check out the bathrooms... they're definitely interesting...I felt like I was in an airplane. Kinda strange, but fun.
label: POS

text: This might be the greasiest, indulgent, and unhealthy burger joint in St. Louis and I have to say from the bottom of my heart, I Fucking Love This Place! There are numerous locations all over the city and in the counties so pretty much anywhere you are in St. Louis you are bound to run into one of these bad boys. They serve some insanely good milkshakes with tons of interesting flavors (from lime to chocolate fudge) and have great steak burgers (a steak burger is supposedly a mixture of different kinds of "premium" beef). Steak n' Shakes are open 24 hours a day and have been the place to go after a hard night of partying since I could see over a bar. So the next time you find yourself with a wicked case of the munchies, roll by one of these great fast food joints!

text: I'm solely rating this on food, so let me say that it seems a decent hangout for the college kids. Distressed leather chairs, fireplace, free wi-fi, and decent coffee. And I hate to give them such a low rating as I found the staff really helpful and attentive and I really wanted to like this place. But outside of that? Things went downhill. The beignet's are ok, especially the chocolate (small dollop of dark chocolate inside). As for the comment about Cafe Du Monde? Not even close. But for St. Louis you probably won't find better. Only other bright spot would have been the Muffaleta sandwich. I had high hopes for the Cuban and the Portabello but they were nothing special. The "crab cakes" seemed to be a highlighted item on the menu so we ordered a couple of those too. These were cream cheese and blue crab meat inside of a tiny tart style pastry. The consistency inside was similar to a quiche, very little crab (or even flavor of crab), and the pastry was a letdown. The remoulade that it came with was actually pretty good and could have improved the dish, but there was barely a drizzle used as a dressing on the small salad on the plate much less any to use on the crab concoction. Lobster bisque was virtually inedible. Far too heavy a hand with the cream, and a bit more tomato would have balanced it out a bit more. The stock was simply overwhelming everything. Pricing seemed out of proportion with the quality of offerings, and the college crowd they're likely to see the most of. I'd gladly pay $9 for any of the options we tried *if* the quality was there. It's a shame really as it's a pretty hip space. Now, if you're looking for a alternative to a starbucks and just want some coffee, a pastry, and a place to hang then I'd say go for it. And they stay open late so if you're out on the town and had a bit to drink then maybe not a bad option. But as a eating destination.....?
label: NEG

text: I love this place! Yes...expect the wait and the sharing of table if you don't mind. Why wouldn't you mind? It's about the size of a ping pong ball and they are filled with ground pork inside. Trust me...they are really good and better than the beef. Add vinegar and chili oil. If you don't like soup, get the pork with soy sauce. It has a great base of crunchy lettuce, fresh cooked noodles and a thin but very well seasoned sauce of ground pork. Add some chili oil to it and it will be your favorite noodle dish in Philly. When the weather gets a bit cold and damp, this is all I crave.

text: Sung to the tune of 'Do Your Ears Hang Low' - Seriously. Do your pants run long? Do they drag along the floor? Do you rubberband them up? Do you staple them up yourself? Do you wish there was a tailor That is pretty reasonably priced Well I found you one! I don't think I've ever been able to buy a pair of pants that was actually the right length for me. They're always too long, but most of the time, I buy jeans that are too cheap for me to justify taking them to the tailor. Well, I recently bought a pair of jeans to which I'd like to preserve the integrity of the bottom hem, and since I'm a complete useless person when it comes to sewing things myself, I set out on a trek. I happened across Best Seasons mostly because it's only a block away from my apartment, and I must say, I was pretty lucky. The moment you walk in, you see pants, shirts, tags, and bags lining every nook and cranny of the store, in haphazard yet seemingly organized piles. A happy, older gentleman, with a measuring tape around his neck, spectacles atop his crown, peers over his work, apparently entertaining some friends while he works away. Hemming my pants were $7 each. Average cost of hemming pants apparently is $8-$12. Score. I spoke Mandarin, but he speaks Cantonese, so that was a failed experiment at communication. However, his English is perfectly fine. He asks when I need them by, so I assume he needs a week or something, after taking a glance of all the articles of clothing he has lying around. I tell him I'm in no hurry, and he tells me to come back the following day. He must have elves helping him! In any case, he did a great job, and for $7! I'll definitely be coming back.
label: POS

text: It was about a year ago to the date. I ventured up here with some of my screwball friends looking for laughs, a nice walk, and some coffee to boot. Penn students (who I respectfully recognize hold Yelp down) historically have treated this place like a coffeehouse library... meaning, no talking, no laughing, nothing besides the turning of pages, the discussions of studies, the sound of keyboards, and all that. Famously apathetic, my posse and I started carrying on in here and were promptly shhh'd. By the third shhh, we went outside to sit on the adjacent wall and let the coffee and cold air react together in our lungs. Shortly thereafter, a drunken man fell into me, and sloppily threatened to rob me. Long story short, 15 minutes later, we bid each other adieu with a handshake as he wiped his teary eyes, a better person. My pockets remained fat and not flat, and I ventured back East. Because of its snotty ambiance, I don't often return, unless I want to piss off some diligent students... which I've got better things to do. I do love their late hours and charismatic staff.

text: On a recent Saturday, my husand and I ventured to Casona's for a romantic lunch. Collingswood is a lovely strolling town. Casona's porch is inviting and we were lured in by the music. Little did we know that the service would be so completely lacking. We ordered the ceviche which was truly delicious. After waiting for another 45 minutes, a handsome and polite waiter appeared to tell us that there were no more black beans and inquired if we still wanted the Cuban sandwich that we ordered. Where was our waitress? What happened to the promise that our food would be "right out"? Why did people who sat down only fifteen minutes earlier have their food served so swiftly? The Cuban sandwich was really disappointing. It consisted of very dry and gristly pork with plain deli ham, flavorless sauce and pickle remnants on half the sandwich served up on a wonderful roll. Pretty sad overall! We will never go back and never recommend this restaurant. Our waitress did not check back to see if we enjoyed our meal or if there was anything to make our experience 5-star. She vanished until it was time to give us our check. I believe that the F-troop was on duty this Saturday. Very disappointing overall. P.U.

text: Flyers + beer + a win == yes, guy! In a whirlwind 48 hours in Philly, I managed to squeeze in a Flyers game on a chilly Saturday afternoon against the hapless Devils. The tailgate parties must be out of control. In relation to the other hockey venues I've been to (Ottawa, Toronto, Buffalo, NYC), the Wells-Fargo Centre seating is really primo. Seating in Toronto and Ottawa is terrible from the second deck, Buffalo is a close second and NYC was decent. A side note about Flyers fans: you guys rule. I loved the punctuation of "you suck!" after each Jersey player was announced! Hockey without beer would be a sin, so I decided to make my way around the taps here and I couldn't believe my eyes. Sam Adams, Heineken and Stella and only $8? We pay $11 for Canadian and Coors Light in Toronto! Sure it's bigger, but it's far crappier! You've got yourself a great thing here Philadelphia and don't you forget it, but if you do, I'll be back to remind you. Go Flyers!

text: As mentioned in a previous review, I consider myself to have a starwood disorder. I will travel out of my way for precious extra points and the status I usually have at a Starwood hotel. their places tend to be clean, nice, and very service-oriented. And the W line tends to add the right amount of style and swank to make me feel less like I am a 'road warrior' (yes, I have heard people use this retarded phrase) and more like I am on vacation.....until the next morning's 6:00 am meeting but I digress... so when my plans take me to the PHL area (and they often do), I search for an spg hotel to continue this tradition. on the night of all the Beijing spectacle, 8/8/08 also witnessed the opening of starwood's new concept hotel here in Philadelphia - W's aLoft hotel chain - a chain that seems to be popping up in the outskirts and suburbs of cities across the country. and that might be why this place just didn't sit well with me it definitely had some positives - cool, European styling - huge flat screen telly in room - nice tiled shower in bathroom - pool table and other 'young' aspects in the lobby. but it definitely had some problems - it was the loudest damn hotel I have been to in a while - walls, paper-thin - windows facing the highway and airport, definitely not thick enough to block out the noise. it just feels like they threw the place together with a gift card from Ikea - stylin sleak lines and durability of product that will coincidentaly break right about when it goes out of style. Unlike its more mature sibling, the W, this place is definitely the suburban 'trying to act cool' kid brother who still needs to grow out of an awkward phase. and lastly, location. I have already pointed out (hopefully) that this isn't the place you would come for a vacation, but rather a layover of some sort - and if the layover is because of the highly likely occassion that PHL airport has delays and cancellations, you might be OK here. But if you are here longer than a "I just need to crash" period of time, well - you are kind of effed - because this hotel is on a Starwood compound with two other properties - between them hosting 2 restaurants that are along the lines of a $17 burger variety - granted, downtown is only a 15-20 minutes drive away, with many options - but if you want something close by other than said $17 burger (no joke) or something off Mickey D's dollar menu, you are SOL - there is nothing else nearby. Again, this probably follows along the business plan/concept for this chain of hotel - get into a segment of the market where Starwood hotels don't exist - out near airports and suburban and ex-urban locales near office parks and convention centers - and my wondering is "just because there aren't hotels out there, does that necessarily mean there needs to be?" - and if I am using this place as a clue to the answer, my vote would probably be "um, nope"

text: This is the best beer bar in all of Philly. If you don't believe me, check out www.beeradvocate.com and they'll tell you I'm right. Try them, they're hella tasty I love Monks for several reasons. First and foremost is the beer selection. If you're still new to the Belgian beer scene, the bartenders there will have a good idea of what you like, if you give them a hint. The food plays a nice supporting role at Monks. The food is great, but does not outshine the beer. Lets be honest this place is more bar than it is restaurant. I can speak from personal experience that the steak frites, the mussels, the rack of lamb and of course the pom frites are a great compliment to the beer. So if you want a diverse beer selection, knowledgeable bar/wait staff and good food, I would highly recommend monks. Although this place does get a little crowded on Thursday - Saturday nights. text: Oh man oh man. The Gallery. I have a love/hate relationship with the Gallery. I live really close by and I don't have a car, so I find myself for the first time in my life, relying on a shitty K-Mart for a lot of houseware shopping. The K-mart, Burlington Coat Factory or Old Navy may not meet any of my wardrobe expectations, but I found a Hannah Montana iPod dock SLASH guitar amp there and I can safely say it was the only practice amp I could find on Market Street! (Don't worry, I took it back and went to an actual music store.) I can't really say that the stores are terrible... they just cater to a different demographic. (I grew up in southern California in between Fashion Island and South Coast Plaza, two very upscale malls. Theres nothing I want to buy in them either. In fact, when I walk through South Coast Plaza it elicits a very rare urge within me to go all Adbusters-Culure-Jam and destroy everything) It seems pretty racist, however, for a white kid like me to label it 'ghetto'. It's a transient salt-of-the-earth crowd, sure, but theres a Chick-fil-A and a greasy Chinese joint in the food court, and that makes me happy. Sure I could walk 3 blocks in the other direction from my door and eat Chick-fil-A and literally the exact same shitty Chinese at Liberty Place, but whats the fun in that? Not like the Shops at Liberty Place have much to brag about. Godiva and Express are shitty chain stores too. But I digress... I rarely ever utilize the train station component of this urban planning skylark but I often find myself walking through the Gallery when its not so nice outside to get from 12th to 9th Sts. The design of this mall might have looked neat on the drafting table, but it is an absolute disaster. As a relative newcomer to this town, it seems like there was a big push to clean up the city for the bicentennial and then, 33 years later, people are trying to clean it up to finish what they started. It feels pretty disingenuous. But that is why we are left with such gems as the Ben Franklin museum in Franklin Court. I like walking up on the deserted upper levels. There is this video game place up in the eastern corner, it seems like they exist in a weird nether world, unless you know about that place there is literally no reason, aside from mall exploration, to get up into that corner of the mall. Surely people must know about it because it is still in business. The Gallery is a depressing and soulless place, like most malls, but that is part of the charm. The people watching is kind of fun too. I really want to catch happy hour at that mall bar. Talk about soul crushing! I can't imagine the exponential rise in suck that would rain down on this place if they opened a casino. I am actually pretty surprised at the lack of big name luxury malls in Philadelphia. Maybe its just a west coast thing. When I need something that would be very easy to acquire out in the strip mall laden suburbs, I am forced to go to the Gallery to be invariably let down. Tired of feeling great? Take a soul-numbing stroll through the stinky corridors of the Gallery and revel in the stupid shit companies want low-income people to waste money on. And stop by the Cinnabon on your way out.
label: NEG

text: This is my favorite St. Louis restaurant. Not all of the tapas are strict interpretations of traditional Spanish fare, but they're all delightful. I lived in southern Spain (Sevilla) for six months and love the chef's personal touch on the items. The cocktail menu is also fun and includes variety. Service is usually good, even when they're packed. Tapas come out as they're ready, so you're rarely without some new treat on the table. text: 2100 Parkway is a gorgeous apartment building with a great location. It is the old 1930's Philadelphia School Administration Building located next door to the Franklin Institute. The building seems to attract good people and the people that work there are great including the door (wo)men, maintenance folks, and property manager. The best thing about this building: they allow pets and it seems like most tenants have dogs. The rent seems to be comparable for the value and location, if not a little less expensive. The units are recently renovated with new appliances and a washer/dryer in the unit. The perks include a gym in the basement and a bike storage room, although storage is otherwise very limited. One thing worth noting is the ceiling height. The units on the first two floors have loft celings, whereas the other floors all appear to have a significantly lower ceiling height, although I haven't seen the secretive 11th floor to which the elevators don't go. Another thing to note are the windows. All units have fabulous huge windows, but in some units they don't open and in some units the configuration doesn't allow the presence of a screen so opening your windows is opening your place to the elements. And its a little odd, but there are at least two businesses that also call 2100 Parkway home. There's an architecture firm in the west wing on the 2nd floor, and the other business is in the east wing of the first floor and has its own separate entrance. I had heard mixed reviews of the management, but we've only had positive experiences with them, including the property manager who has been very helpful and responsive. Its a great building overall.
