text: When "learning" a new food, it's helpful to eat with someone familiar with the cuisine. My friend Lori acted as my willing guide to the SH. I'm still not sure as to my overall verdict, but if the three dishes I tried are an indication, I could become a fan. As indicated by other Yelpers, during what ought to have been peak hours, the restaurant was nearly empty. We sat on one side of the main room, one other party sat on the other side. Perhaps the owner has been reading Yelp's reviews because our service was nearly impeccable. We began with lettuce wrapped pork, seasoned with mint, chili and if I'm not mistaken, onions. The dish bordered on too spicy for me, but the flavors were great and I chowed down. From the time we ordered this, to the time it arrived was under 10 minutes. Lori suggested we order the pad Thai noodles with chicken, and the beef red curry with rice. The pad Thai includes peanuts, and we asked for extra. We were brought a monkey dish full to the brim. Pad Thai noodles are the rice noodle equivalent of spaghetti. They are lighter than chow mein, more substantial than glass noodles. SH uses only the white chicken meat in the dish. The garnish consists of fresh green onions. Very flavorful and yet extremely delicate. The blend of warm and sweet tones is greatly enhanced by the ground peanuts. The Red Curry is served in a large soup bowl. Rice accompanies it in a separate bowl. Meat and sauce are spooned over the rice. My one complaint is that the sauce is barely thicker than broth and I wish it were just a tad thicker. It's sweet and hot, but not too hot. Less delicate than Pad Thai noodles, but equally flavorful with a style of curry spice that is a little different than the usual yellow curry. Compared with Chinese food, Thai food is prepared using little oil. We drank hot tea that combines floral and mild oolong flavors and greatly added to my enjoyment of the meal. Throughout the dinner, our service was spot on -- with one exception. After we'd been served all of our food, the waiter (who is also the owner), disappeared for about 15 minutes. I wanted to pay and go. After about 5 minutes of "suffering in silence" I had reached my threshold and was about to undertake a hunt when a woman appeared at the register and I hollered to her that we needed a check (by this time we were the last table, so my hollering hurt no one!). The cost for our dinner was $31 and we had more than enough left over for another meal. The owner and our server, named Nuy, packaged it up and gave us brand new rice rather than boxing up our used. Thoughtful. Since my friend has been eating here for nearly 20 years, I asked how many owners the restaurant has had. Nuy is the third or fourth owner. Then he asked if we had a few minutes, and we said we did. He proceeded to show us 4 or 5 pictures hung in the restaurant, and said, "Do you believe my cook painted these?" Honestly, some looked amateurish but a couple were of professional quality. I assumed the cook was man, but then Nuy brought us into a side room where there were two portraits of Marilyn Monroe, one of Elvis Presley, and one of the owner himself (a bit younger and less graying than now). Most interestingly he now referred to the cook as SHE. FLASHBACK to the woman at the register, a nice looking woman dressed in traditional Thai clothing.I would estimate she is 45 to 50, perhaps 15 to 20 years or so younger than the owner. Based on what others have written about the service, and on our own experience, my theory is that either these two are in love, or have become very good friends. He certainly admires her, beaming whenever he brags about her talents. It's actually very sweet. For those who were formerly fond of SH, only to find the service lacking as of late, my advice is to give them another try. Don't be shy. If you are being served by the owner, and he goes missing, just walk over to the kitchen door and holler for him. You can get away with that here. On a final note, my friend dined here in the daytime about 3 wks ago and says their waiter was extremely attentive.

text: Went here last night after picking up a $50 gift certificate from www.restaurant.com. This is a long review but I felt that you should all be informed. (not very inviting) Was met by who I assume was the owner in a ballcap. t-shirt and faded torn jeans. He took us to our table, on the way to the table I noticed the odd sci-fi artwork (not very soothing). Lighting was poor and no candles or flowers on the table. Second Impression: One waitress to serve the entire restaurant? (We felt for the waitress since we saw her running the entire time working to satisfy everyone. She was great!) Looking through the menu we decided to try two glasses of wine Cartlidge & Browne Cab and a Zin. Both were served too warm and the Zin was so acidic we sent it back for a Malbec we had tasted before. (We decided to skip the "by the glass" experience and go with a 2001 Turley Juvenile - HIGHLIGHT OF THE NIGHT) We ordered the Caprese salad with Balsamic Reduction - we received a plate with tomatoes that were not ripe, regular balsamic,three leaves of basil and no seasoning. We looked around for salt and pepper and had to flag down the owner so he could bring a small diner style salt shaker and a large pepper grinder (which he did not leave at the table.) We ordered the NY Steak (med-rare) and the white pizza with four cheeses. We received NY Steak (med-well with gristle and oily veggies) and a sad pizza with red sauce and it looked like maybe two cheeses but surely not worth $12 and not a white pizza. Lasting Impression: Even with the $50 restaurant.com certificate the bill was over $100 and so not worth it. When the wine is the best part of the dining experience it is cheaper to stay home and we never have to ask for Salt & Pepper or candles on the table. This is the reason restaurants fail within the first two years. Good bye 275 Hill.

The recipe was different from what I'm used to, being from Maine (it involved green peppers), but it was quite good; I was surprised, however, that the cakes themselves were squishy and not crispy on the outside. text: Pure can mean so many things...sweet, innocent, undiluted. But I don't think any of these descriptions refer to Pure Nightclub. Then again, I suppose none of the aforementioned reasons are why people go to nightclubs to begin with, especially this one, so maybe that's a good thing. I have made a discovery about myself during my pursuit to Yelp about the things that make Philadelphia so great: I am just not a nightclub kind of gal. Dive bars? Yes, please. Good, creative restaurants? Absolutely. Anywhere where I can get excellent customer service and a good story to take with me? Sign me up. But nightclubs? Just not my thing. But on that note, Pure is a good example of what so many dancey clubs try hard to be. It's big (three floors). There are lots of bars. The music is loud. There is a coat check. And the big booths on the main dance floor offer optimum people watching space. But they also do a bunch of things that didn't make me feel so thrilled, either. Drinks are EXPENSIVE. Crazy expensive. It wasn't that crowded (even though I was there on a Saturday night until after 1'ish, although I know they also do after-hours, so maybe it was too early, just not for me). There was one small room upstairs where people were dancing, but I wasn't feeling the music. And the bathrooms. Yuck. Well, I tried. It just didn't take. So look for me at a bar near you, reasonably priced microbrew and french fries in hand, anxiously anticipating hearing some song that doesn't make me want to hurl. Because there are many things I love about this city. This nightclub just isn't one of them.

For things like contact lenses, I don't really care where I go, as long as I can get these suckers at the best price possible. The nice thing about getting your contacts from a Walmart is that your script is kept in the Walmart system. text: I was vacationing in Santa Barbara with my mother for my birthday and I wanted to have seafood for dinner, so we cruised around by foot near the waterfront, hoping to find a good seafood place to eat. We crossed paths with FisHouse and thought we might as well give it a try. When we entered the restaurant, we were quickly and kindly seated by the host. The atmosphere is "casual/formal", I would say. I wouldn't feel weird coming in with a pair of jeans but I also wouldn't feel overdressed coming in with a skirt. Natural lighting flowed into the restaurant, so it wasn't a dim place. Once we were seated, the waiter came, introduced himself, asked us what we'd like to drink, came back with some bread, and served us our drinks (he was attentive throughout the meal). We decided not to order any appetizers because we didn't want to get too full. When it was time to order, I ordered penne with salmon and vodka sauce and my mother ordered a type of seafood soup, both of which came in less than twenty minutes. This was the first time I've ever eaten pasta with vodka sauce, and I was quite pleased. The pasta wasn't swimming in too much sauce, but it wasn't dry and it wasn't too rich, either. The salmon was sliced into bite-size chunks, and there was an adequate amount (not just a small sprinkling of salmon meat). The peas added a lovely bit of color to the pasta and the dish was presented nicely in a bowl/plate hybrid, which made it easier to eat (I didn't have to worry about my sauce escaping the plate). The portion was good and I ended up taking some of the leftovers with me. I can't say much about the seafood soup my mother ordered, but she said it was delicious, so I'll take her word for it (she's an excellent cook, so I trust her). Since it was my birthday, my mother requested for a dessert at the end of our meal and sure enough, our waiter arrived with a mocha ice cream cake slice (not too big, not too small) drizzled with chocolate fudge, topped with strawberry slices, sprinkled with thinly sliced almonds and garnished with mint. It was delicious, simple, and the right amount I needed after a filling plate of pasta with cream sauce. When we got the check, we were curious to see if the waiter charged us for the dessert and it turned out that he didn't. The cost of our meal was decent overall. For me, it wasn't bad for a first experience, which was great for a birthday meal!

text: DEPRESSED? Think first before asking for HELP... I have a disturbing story. It is a story about basic rights and civil rights and being afraid for my safety. It is about cruelty, abuse, but most importantly, clear civil rights violations at the MONTGOMERY COUNTY EMERGENCY SERVICES (MCES) in Norristown, PA. In early Fall, I walked voluntarily into MCES. I was feeling depressed following a catastrophic illness of a significant other and then a failed job search. I turned to what I "thought" was a crisis center, that would offer me some direction. I just wanted help. In particular, I had been having a daunting experience obtaining outpatient therapy -- one that would accept my insurance coverage. Clearly, this was contributing to my depression. Again, I went VOLUNTARILY to MCES. I was hoping it would provide a "jumpstart" to locating outpatient therapy. I had never gone there previously. I am new to Montgomery County. In retrospect, it is clear now that I walked into the wrong place. During an exchange (intake) with a disturbingly slovenly-dressed, unkempt physician, when it became uncomfortably clear to me that he was paying no attention whatsoever to my verbalization of feelings, I politely asserted myself by addressing this fact (in a non-confrontational manner) -- that I could see he was not listening. He became inflamed. The next thing I knew he accused me of, and labeled me "Hostile". This doctor berated and insulted me in the most demeaning and disgustingly [creepy] condescending tone. I have reported him to the State Board of Medical Licensing. It was egregious, offensive, and absolutely crossed the line. He proceeded to abruptly abort the intake. Then, to my shock and disbelief, he stated "we're done here". This doctor then instructed another employee to "start papers to lock me up on what they called a "302", which they told me means INVOLUNTARY commitment. I was not allowed to leave! He had made this personal. I was horrified and scared out of my mind! I had never in my life had this happen to me! I went there for hope and someone to talk to. I was in pain. And then the nightmare began...There is so much more to disclose about the horrendously poor quality of care at this facility, but since my space is limited here, I will try to summarize the remainder of my nightmare. The adjective "horrific" does not come close to describing my experience. I was improperly placed in a unit with psychotics, criminals, ex-cons and drug addicts. I was terrified. MCES's entire Mission Statement reads, "All individuals will be welcomed and treated in a respectful, professional manner." Despite these claims, there was neither "dignity" nor "respect" to speak of. I have filed the appropriate Grievances. PLEASE be cautious when choosing a crisis center. text: We went for an early table on New Years eve. Usually the best time to hit a restaurant before they get overly busy. The restaurant was almost empty when we arrived - there were 5 front of the house staff available for the 6 tables. The seafood was subpar at best. We started with the Chilled Seafood Pleateau. For $60 - Maine Lobster, King Crab, Oysters, Clams, Lump Crab Meat, Shrimp Cocktail, Tuna Tartare. The seafood plateau arrived at a bare table - dropped off by one of the runners - and that was it. We had to ask for plates and a cracker to get past the shells. The lobster and crab meat were fine. The shrimp over cooked, the tuna stringy, the oysters small and the clams to fishy smelling to eat for our taste. This was a fast food version of a seafood tower after the one we had for our anniversary at the William Douglas steakhoust in Cherry Hill, NJ. That was the BEST we have ever had - the seafood so fresh and amazing. Next we tried the Hot Plateau seafood tower for $50. Crab Cakes, Roast Oysters,Steamed King Crab, Crispy Calamari,Coconut Shrimp, Steamed Mussels, and Clams Casino. It arrived at a table full of dirty dishes and it was amusing to watch the runner attemping to put another tower onto a full table. We not only had to ask him to return to take items off of the table but also for additional clean plates. The Hot Plateau was inedible! No crabcakes. The oysters had a burnt color to the breadcrumbs and a scorched butter smell. The clams looked exactly like the small oysters. The steamed mussels were in a very spicy curry sauce. The calamari were heavily battered and at best were a cheap premade frozen varity. This was sent back - enough was enough. The service was weak and inattentive. The food was not fresh by any standard. The manager - never even one trip through the dining room! Not worth the $100 spent!

Even though she had some bad news for me (I have cavities), she made the cleaning/checkup totally painless. Dr. Strohmeyer is really nice, and super professional. text: Since my friend and I were going to spend all day downtown, we decided Rooster would be a great place to fuel up for our long day. With a restaurant.com coupon in hand, we got to enjoy one breakfast entree, a savory crepe, a dessert crepe, and a cup of coffee all for just $22 (tax and tip included). My friend opted for the rooster slinger, a smorgasbord of eggs, andouille sausage, and breakfast potatoes served on toast and ladled with sausage gravy. I had a few bites and it was spicy -- not too spicy that it had me grabbing for my water but just enough that I could feel the burn. I had the marinated spicy chicken crepe, served with arugula and fontina cheese. The size of the crepe was perfect -- I didn't get sick of it and didn't wonder halfway through, "geez, when's this crepe going to end?". Plus, it left me just enough room to enjoy a dessert crepe with my friend! And on to the star of the meal: the smores crepe. Just as delectable as it sounds. Crumbled cookies, dark chocolate, and marshmallow all wrapped up in a crepe. Every bite was just as delicious as the last. Rooster has a pretty extensive menu of savory and sweet crepes -- and for those who don't want to eat things wrapped in a thin pancake, Rooster also offers a variety of salads, sandwiches, and breakfast entrees. I will definitely be back to try more of their other food offerings and to have another one of those delicious smores crepes!

text: I work locally in Bala Cynwyd and have tired of all the chain restaurants. A week ago I tried Tommy Gunns and it was the best BBQ I have ever had. Now I will preface this statement by saying that I have never had BBQ in Memphis, the Carolina's or Kansas City, but the pulled pork sandwich that I had was orgasmic. The place is small and it was very, very hot inside (but they were smoking meat). I order the pulled pork sandwich and a side of corn bread and took it back to my office. Five minutes into my meal I had co-workers congregating by my desk due to the smell. The pulled pork was so good that I really did not even need the BBQ sauce. I did use the sauce, but I used it sparingly. The pork was juicy and full of flavor. It had a great smoked flavor without being too overpowering. The role appeared to have some glaze on it and was tasty as well. The portion was large as the pulled pork was spilling over the side. I could eat this sandwich every day- that is how good it was. The cornbread was delicious as well and was a great compliment to the sandwich. I have not been to Sweet Lucy's in the Northeast as of yet, but Tommy Gunns is amazing and should be a must stop if you are a BBQ lover.

text: I don't see what others see in Sagami. I think Mikado is better and would probably consider it the best in the Cherry Hill area. The first time I went here, I remember not liking whatever I had, though I can't remember what it was (some sort of fried chicken thing that looked like KFC rather than the tempura coating I would have assumed it would have). I went back and tried some other things on the menu, and I was quite impressed. The shogayaki and negimaki in particular are excellent (I've never seen "shogayaki" served elsewhere... perhaps it's a variant on sukiyaki?) Their sushi is very fresh tasting and it looked like they had some interesting rolls, though I didn't order anything extravagant in the sushi dept. Their soup is above average, but not the best I've ever tried, but their salad is quite good. The dressing has a bit of a nutty flavor that others lack. I don't think the Cherry Hill one has Hibachi, but their Mt. Laurel location does. I only tried the hibachi there once, but the food came out great, even though the chef seemed rather tired that day. Not *quite* as good as Arirang, but *much* cheaper, and there isn't an Arirang anywhere near here besides :) Their prices are also excellent, particularly on the lunch menu. You can get a fairly large lunch meal for $7-$8, which is very good for Japanese food. I'd strongly recommend it.

text: I'd been fishing all day and when it was finally 12:32am, I just needed food. My body needed it all; proteins, fats, and carbohydrates. For the carbs, I wanted beer. My friends were at a bar nearby that doesn't really serve food, so I needed to find an option for the fats and protein. Fried chicken. Grabbed a 3 piece box consisting of a wing, thigh, and breast from Lincoln just a few blocks away. I'm here to tell you that I'm sorry that I did. I live near a CFC (Crown) and they serve a good bird. I thought all of these loosely similar but independently-owned chicken joints had a similar recipe, or even quality control. Boy was I wrong. When I got to the bar and slugged two city specials, I was ready to eat. I wish I had stopped by a Wawa on the way back from fishing. The seasoning, or lack-there-of, was paltry. The breast piece had to have been sitting under a lamp for at least 8 hours. My jaws still kind of hurt from chewing and gnawing. Of course I ate it all, I was hungry. But the fact that I was so hungry and kinda drunk and am still complaining just tells you how bad the chicken was. text: Wasabi is a great place for sushi in St. Louis and it's probably one of the most reasonably priced, too. If you're feeling adventurous (and not very frugal), I would check out their "tours of" menu choices. These complete meals are pretty pricey but feature the freshest fish and are a great way to sample the menu all at once. The wine list here is great, too, and the friendly wait staff is always ready with a suggested pairing. Wasabi can be a great place to grab a quick, fairly cheap, sushi lunch or indulge in an expensive, elegant dinner. Either way, you won't be disappointed.

text: What can even be said about Olympia that will sound like I actually do not hate every restaurant in the St Louis area? Probably not much. Here goes nothing: Olympia has decent food. They do, I admit it willingly (I can post a picture showing there is no gun to my head if needed). End thought. Olympia does not under any definition of the word or idea serve Greek food. There, I said it. Please bring on the verbal deluge. You just cannot claim to be a Greek restaurant and serve a mediocre on its best day gyro, and the other crap they hand out here. If you would like to re-brand yourself as a bar Olympia, I would probably still not go to you again, because even for that it is too far off of my beaten path, and I can get bar food anywhere. The menu breakdown. Appetizers. "Flaming Cheese"? Oh you mean Saganaki? At least you are using the right kind of cheese, but I am put off by this. "Hermes Hot Wings"? If I serve everything I make with a poorly made tzatziki can I name it after historic Greek figures? Main course. Burgers do not belong on a menu at a Greek restaurant. You would think that would be the end of this portion but no. There is also the chicken fingers option. Did I come to a Greek restaurant or a burger joint? I also really have no idea what was put in the moussaka or pastitsio... but when I make these in my own kitchen they taste more Greek than this. Oh wait, that might be because I have an actual recipe for these and not the Wikipedia entry. Dessert. "Baklava". I really think the quotes say it all. I understand this is a hard dish to master. But just don't put it on your menu. Or better yet, stop calling yourself a Greek food restaurant. If you are looking for a gyro, go to Delmar, Gyro House is the place for you. If you are looking for other Greek specialties, then you are going to have to bear with me, because so am I... The once yearly St Nicholas GreekFest is not enough to hold me over. And until I can find a suitable alternative I am going to keep cooking my best friend's grandmother's pastitsio recipe. If you are craving some, let me know, I will invite you over. Probably charge less too.

text: My family and I booked a room at the Saddlebrook Resort Spa this past weekend and had a lackluster experience. It wasn't a horrendous experience but I would not recommend this place to others. From the outside, the buildings look a bit dated but the rooms themselves were updated and comfortable. The bad taste of this resort was in their lack of customer service and valet. My first real gripe was at the valet stand up front. You have to get your car valeted when you come and go. You cannot easily access your room from where they park the cars (it's too far away.) They also provide golf cart shuttles to get you to your room. I found it inconvenient I had to tip a valet every time I wanted to go somewhere. The most infuriating instance was when I pulled my car up with my family. I asked to leave the car up front for an hour so we could change our clothes and clean up before leaving to go grab dinner. The valets said that we couldn't leave the car there and they would need to park it. The valet instructed for me to leave the car running and he would go and park it. I came back an hour later to leave and they couldn't find my car for a while (the valet never gave me a ticket.) I wait, I wait.... I wait and then the car rolls up and finally we leave. On my way to the restaurant, I notice that my gas tank is bone dry empty! I knew that I had a little less than a quarter tank when I dropped my car off with the valet which could only mean that they had left that car running for a very LONG period of time before they finally drove it to a spot. During our stay, I had to request clean towels 3 separate times and still never received them. On top of everything else, the resort had the audacity to charge a $10 per night valet fee that I was not aware of in advance. I found out by noticing the itemized charge on my bill when checking out.
label: NEG

Experience real New Orleans food, don't even bother stopping here for the kitschy film stuff.

text: We had no idea this was a Starr restaurant until we saw "STARR" postcards by the door as we left. Stella had no "Starr" quality. We thought it was a slightly better looking than average, decent quality, grossly overpriced "New York Style (wink wink)" pizza place that would thrive in it's location due to outdoor seating. First there is nothing on the menu about the size of the pizza. This is important. The extremely thin crust, sparsely topped, brittle pies came in one size, one usually considered "small." Neither the menu nor our server mentioned this. Our server came over 3 times to take our order and never offered any info or assistance as we wrangled with the menu. Prices ranged from $10 to $17 per pizza. We assumed splitting one would be a meal. Many of the pizza combinations seemed more creative than complementary. The "special pizza" with ramps sounded delicious but tender, delicate, seasonal ramps were paired with asparagus which upon roasting would overwhelm the ramps. We ordered thru a similar process of elimination. We have adventurous palettes but respect ingredients and don't eat as a "dare" preferring harmony. We got a meatball pie with ricotta, mozzarella and fresh basil and a romaine salad to split. The service was "hovery" but not good. A server should stand still when they ask "is everything ok." When we did have a question -if goat cheese was in the "Romaine salad" we were served, our server said "No, it's Ricotta (garbled)" haughtily turned on her heel and left. We both loathe goat cheese but picked around whatever the hell it was and enjoyed the salad. The red onions and hints of mint worked well together. The romaine and tomatoes were fresh. The casual food and decor clashes with the constant clearing, of dishes, especially those still in use. Philadelphia kitchens have come to rely more and more on fewer and fewer Philadelphians and Stella is no exception. Sad to see a South Street "open kitchen" wood fired, brick oven pizza being completely staffed by people who chattered loudly in Spanish. That brought the "authentic wood fired pizza experience" down several notches. The interior was stylish but not outstanding. The personalized wood burning oven screamed look at me. The bathrooms were clean but rather pedestrian. The newly renovated Melrose Diner's ladies room with glass tile is more stylishly appointed. The muzak was ironic, mixing the Jam with Fleetwood Mac. We had just finished our salad when the pizza came. We both laughed. It was tiny. The crust was highly visible. At the first bite we could tell this pizza was a New York joke on South Street patrons. It was literally a "meatball pizza" it perhaps had ONE thinly shaved meatball on the whole thing. The crust was floury, tortilla thin, crackly and artfully appointed with toppings. It was tasty, tiny, extremely expensive and unsatisfying. While swatting away staff who kept trying to take our plates while we swiftly ate the pizza we announced our verdict on Stella, SUCKS and is for SUCKERS. There was mounting tension and disappointment as we realized we both were still hungry, but didn't want to order another precious pizza. We considered our portions equivalent to a "light lunch." Our server, or a size on the menu could have guided us better. Really easy fixes. We were STUNNED to find out it was a Starr place as we left. Only 2 clues it was a Starr place, the choice of bottled or ice water and ramps as a feature ingredient. The cost per portion should have been a clue. After we settled up, we took our starving selves to Phileo.

text: A fairly new place in the Clearwater area this is a wonderful restaurant. The owner is Bolivian and it really comes through. Clearwater has a serious lacking of authentic Spanish places (especially compared to Tampa) and Pico Rojo is a welcome addition. The chicken is marinated over night and cooked over natural charcoal. I have NEVER had a piece of chicken as juicy as this was. We also had some fried cheese which was nice, steak fries, and yucca fries which were OUTSTANDING. The chicken is served with a combination of sauces which also really enhance the flavor. It has a nice pleasant atmosphere and the staff is very friendly. Beer and wine and a plethora of drinks are also available. We will definitely be going back soon and often.
